articles.body_html:
Hoi hoi!

YAY! is-kit just reached 100 GitHub stars⭐ 🎉🎉🎉

When it reached 50 stars, I wrote about how we use it in a production TypeScript application serving more than 100,000 users. 👇

is-kit Reached 50 Stars ⭐ Here’s How We Use It in Production
Real-world scale for type safety
nyaomaru
nyaomaru
Aug 12

is-kit Reached 50 Stars ⭐ Here’s How We Use It in Production

#typescript #opensource #webdev #frontend
97 reactions Comments 21 comments
7 min read

I could write the same story again. But that would be boring. 😹

A lot has happened since then.

The library gained new APIs, some existing APIs became stricter, I started using it in more of my own OSS projects, and one real-world use case even exposed a type inference edge case in Effect.

So this time, instead of explaining the production adoption again, I want to look at:

  • What changed between 50 and 100 stars
  • Some of the most important APIs added since then
  • How I am actually using is-kit outside the original production application
  • A real bug report involving Effect.catchIf
  • What 100 stars means to me now

Let's dive in! 🔧

⭐ First, What Did 50 Stars Mean?

At 50 stars, the biggest thing I wanted to show was that is-kit was not only a toy project.

It was already being used in a real production application. 🚀

The application had repeated runtime checks like

typeof value === "string";
typeof value === "number";
value === null || value === undefined;

and several larger user-defined type guards for things like HTTP errors, literal unions, arrays, API values, and plain objects.

The interesting part was not that is-kit made those checks shorter.
The interesting part was that it gave them one reusable shape.

Small guards could be composed.

Application-owned helpers could sit between the library and feature code. And the result could still participate in normal TypeScript control flow.

That part has not changed.

But since 50 stars, the library itself has moved quite a bit. 👀

🔑 Property Refinement Became a First-Class Use Case

One thing I kept running into was this.

I already have a good type guard.
I just want to apply it to one property.

For example

declare const input: unknown;

Maybe I already know how to validate a string

import { isString } from "is-kit";

But now I want to express

"This object has a name property, and that property is a string."

That sounds simple, but there are actually a few different cases.

A required property is not the same as an optional property.
An array index is not the same as an object property.

And an optional property that becomes known to be defined should narrow differently from one that is still optional.

So is-kit added three property refinement helpers:

  • refineKey
  • refineDefinedKey
  • refineIndex

The idea is simple

Take a type guard you already trust and lift it onto a property or array element.

For example

import { isString, refineKey } from "is-kit";

const hasStringName = refineKey("name", isString);

Now the string guard is reusable at a deeper level instead of being rewritten inside another custom predicate.

This is a small API, but I like it because it follows the same design goal as the rest of is-kit.

Do not build one giant validator.

Build small checks that can be reused in normal TypeScript code.

🔍 Then discriminatedUnion Got Much More Serious

The biggest addition since the 50-star article is probably the exhaustive discriminated union API introduced in v1.15.0.

Consider a common TypeScript type

type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };

At runtime, validating this is not difficult.

You can check ok, then validate the corresponding fields.

But there is another question

Can TypeScript verify that the validator itself covers the whole union?

That is where discriminatedUnion comes in.

import { discriminatedUnion, isString, oneOfValues, typedStruct } from "is-kit";

type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };

const resultUnion = discriminatedUnion<Result>();

export const isResult = resultUnion("ok", [true, false], {
  true: typedStruct<Extract<Result, { ok: true }>>()({
    ok: oneOfValues(true),
    value: isString,
  }),
  false: typedStruct<Extract<Result, { ok: false }>>()({
    ok: oneOfValues(false),
    error: isString,
  }),
});

The runtime behavior is useful.

But the more interesting part is the compile-time contract.

The builder checks things like:

  • Missing discriminant branches
  • Extra branches
  • Incompatible branch guards
  • Incomplete discriminant tuples

So if the union changes, the guard cannot silently stay incomplete.

That matters because one of the easiest ways for a hand-written type guard to become dangerous is drift.

The TypeScript type evolves.
The runtime guard does not.
And the compiler cannot normally tell you that the two are no longer aligned.

discriminatedUnion is one attempt to make that class of mistake harder.

💪 The Library Also Became Stricter

Not every improvement between 50 and 100 stars was a new feature.

A lot of work was about making existing behavior more precise.

For example, recent releases included fixes around:

  • recordOf literal-key narrowing
  • native Error brand checks
  • array guards with overridden iterators
  • exact struct validation
  • symbol-keyed struct schemas
  • cross-realm struct schemas

There was also more package-level testing.

is-kit now checks published-package behavior from both ESM and CommonJS TypeScript consumers, and also has Deno / JSR smoke coverage.

This part is less exciting to show in a code snippet.

But for a small library, I think it is important.

Making sure they behave correctly in weird JavaScript and TypeScript environments is where things become real.

🤖 I Started Using is-kit in Other OSS Too

Since reaching 50 stars, I've also started using is-kit more naturally in other OSS projects I maintain.

For example, in my changelog tooling of changelog-bot, I use define to keep small predicates reusable and composable instead of turning every runtime check into an isolated helper.

A simplified example looks like this 👇

import { define, oneOfValues } from "is-kit";

const CHANGELOG_SECTIONS = ["Added", "Changed", "Fixed", "Removed"] as const;

const isChangelogSection = define<(typeof CHANGELOG_SECTIONS)[number]>(
  oneOfValues(CHANGELOG_SECTIONS),
);

The exact code is not the important part.

What changed for me is that I no longer think

"I should use my library here."

I just reach for the guard I need.

A library starts becoming useful to its maintainer when it stops feeling like a demo of itself.

🚀 Then an is-kit Guard Ran Into an Effect Type Bug

This was one of the most interesting things that happened recently.

An is-kit user was using a type guard with Effect's catchIf.

Conceptually, the refinement looked like this 👇

(error: unknown): error is SomeError => ...

That is completely normal for is-kit.

In fact, unknown is exactly where the library is designed to start.

But with Effect.catchIf, that refinement could affect generic inference in an unexpected way.

The error channel could become widened to unknown.

The reported case resulted in this Effect PR 👏 And merged 🚀

fix(effect): Made catchIf NoInfer Refinement's first arg with generic Err param #9252

nikelborm posted on Oct 15, 2026

Type

  • [ ] Refactor
  • [ ] Feature
  • [x] Bug Fix
  • [ ] Optimization
  • [ ] Documentation Update

Description

When passing (arg: unknown) => arg is SomeError to some catchIfs, it turned the error channel into unknown. This PR makes only self's Error slot influence the types, regardless of the type taken by refinement.

Validation: the Channel, Effect, and Stream type-test files pass on TypeScript 5.9.3 and 6.0.3, and pnpm check passes. Temporarily reverting the implementation reproduces unknown error-channel widening in Channel data-last usage and in unrelated-refinement cases across all three APIs. The matching data-first refinement cases also pass without the fix. No tests were changed during maintainer validation.

Closes EFF-2233

View on GitHub

The relevant type originally looked roughly like this

refinement: Predicate.Refinement<E, EB>;

and the fix changed it to

refinement: Predicate.Refinement<NoInfer<E>, EB>;

The important idea is that the refinement's input type should not be allowed to redefine the error type already established by the Effect.

The PR also adds type tests for cases like

const result = Effect.catchIf(
  mixedEffect,
  (e: unknown): e is AiError => e instanceof AiError,
  () => Effect.succeed("ok"),
);

Without the fix, the refinement input could participate in inference and widen the error channel.

With NoInfer, the original error type remains the source of truth.

The same pattern was fixed for Channel and Stream too.

There was also a Bluesky post about the issue

Not like the lib itself caught it, but when I created a reusable operator: export const isNotFoundError = and( isObject, refineDefinedKey('reason', equalsKey('_tag', 'NotFound')), ) I noticed my streams having unknown in the error channel github.com/Effect-TS/ef...

— Evangeline Rome 🌵🦎🌱🐢🐍🐸 🥦 (@evadeva.bsky.social) 2026-10-15T16:38:16.787Z

I really liked this bug because it came from an interaction I would probably never have discovered by testing is-kit alone.

is-kit did not "break Effect". And Effect was not doing something absurd either.

It was a subtle TypeScript inference interaction between a generic API and a refinement whose input was intentionally broad.

That is exactly the kind of edge case that appears when libraries start meeting each other in real code.

👍 This Is the Kind of Feedback I Wanted

When is-kit reached 50 stars, I wrote

"Someone found this idea useful."

That was already enough to make me happy.

100 stars still does not mean the library is huge.

A star is still not a benchmark.
It is still not proof of correctness.
And it definitely does not mean every TypeScript project should install is-kit.

But something has changed.

People are not only starring the repository anymore.

They are

  • Using the library
  • Asking questions
  • Finding edge cases
  • Reporting bugs
  • Comparing it with other validation approaches
  • Using its guards with other TypeScript libraries
  • Making me reconsider APIs I thought were already finished

That is much more valuable than the number itself. 💖

💬 The Project Is Also Becoming Easier to Explain

Another thing changed between 50 and 100 stars.

I became much clearer about what is-kit is not.

It is not trying to replace every schema library.
It is not trying to turn every runtime value into a schema-first workflow.
And it is not trying to hide normal TypeScript control flow.

The core question is still very small

"Can this unknown value safely enter this branch?"

Sometimes a schema library is the right answer.

For example, if I need:

  • Rich validation errors
  • Transformations
  • Form validation
  • A contract shared across systems

I may want Zod, Valibot, ArkType, or something else.

But sometimes I already have normal TypeScript code and I only need a reusable narrowing function.

That is where I want is-kit to be useful.

if (isUser(value)) {
  value.id;
}

if (isHttpClientError(error)) {
  // Handle HTTP client errors
}

items.filter(isString);

result.catch(isHttpClientError);

const isMaybeNumber = nullish(isNumber);

Small runtime decisions.
Normal functions.
Normal TypeScript.

🐱 What 100 Stars Means to Me

100 stars is still small compared with the largest TypeScript OSS projects.

No problem.

What matters to me is that the project is becoming more real in ways that have nothing to do with the star counter.

Since the 50-star milestone:

  • New APIs were added
  • Existing APIs became stricter
  • Runtime edge cases were fixed
  • Package compatibility testing improved
  • I started using is-kit naturally in other OSS
  • External usage produced feedback I could not generate alone
  • An unknown-based refinement even helped expose an inference edge case in Effect

That last part is probably my favorite.

Because the goal was never to build a library that only looks nice in its own README!!!

The goal is to make reusable runtime narrowing work naturally inside real TypeScript code.

And now I am starting to see that happen outside my own repository too.

Thank you to everyone who starred the project, tried it, reported something, asked a question, opened an issue, or simply read the code. 🙏

There is still a lot I want to improve.

But 100 feels pretty nice. 😸⭐

If small composable type guards fit your TypeScript style, give it a try!

articles.title: In Ruby, Objects Don't Have Methods. How Method Lookup Actually Works.
articles.description: A visual deep dive into Ruby's object model under the hood. Why objects store state but zero methods, how hidden eigenclasses work, and the real method lookup path.
articles.body_html:
Ask almost any developer how object-oriented programming works, and they will describe the same textbook picture: an object bundles data and methods together into a single unit.

In Ruby, you hear this idea reinforced constantly under the slogan: "Everything is an object."

You create a string, call .upcase on it, and it feels completely natural to assume that the string object owns that method. You create a user object, call .save, and assume .save lives inside your user.

Except that is not how Ruby works at all.

In Ruby, objects contain zero methods.

If you inspect an instance down at the C source code level in CRuby (MRI), you discover something surprising: an object stores its instance variables, a set of internal flags, and a pointer to another structure. It does not contain a single line of method code, nor does it contain a method table.

Where do methods actually live? How does Ruby know what to execute when you type user.greet? And what actually happens when you define a method on a single specific object?

To truly master Ruby, you have to look beneath the syntactic sugar and understand the mechanics of Ruby's object model: method tables, the hidden eigenclass, and the ancestry ladder.

The First Surprise: Objects Store State, Classes Store Methods

Let us look at a simple Ruby class:

class User
  def initialize(name, email)
    @name = name
    @email = email
  end

  def greet
    "Hello, I am #{@name}"
  end
end

user = User.new("Alice", "alice@example.com")

When Ruby evaluates User.new, the virtual machine allocates a heap structure called an RObject.

Inside this RObject, Ruby stores two things:

  1. An array of instance variables: @name set to "Alice", and @email set to "alice@example.com".
  2. An internal pointer named klass, pointing directly to the User class object.

Notice what is missing from user: the greet method is nowhere to be found.

Methods in Ruby live exclusively inside classes (represented internally as RClass).

The User class contains a hash table called m_tbl (the method table). When you define def greet, Ruby writes an entry into User's method table mapping the symbol :greet to its compiled bytecode body.

When you call user.greet:

  1. Ruby does not look inside user.
  2. Ruby follows user's internal klass pointer to the User class.
  3. Ruby searches User's m_tbl for :greet.
  4. It finds the method and executes it in the context of self = user.

This separation is what makes Ruby memory-efficient. You can instantiate one hundred thousand User objects, and all one hundred thousand share the exact same method table inside User. The instances only hold their personal instance variables.

The Mystery of Singleton Methods

Now consider this famous Ruby feature: you can add a method to just one individual object without affecting any other instance of that class.

str1 = "hello"
str2 = "world"

def str1.shout
  upcase + "!!!"
end

str1.shout #=> "HELLO!!!"
str2.shout #=> NoMethodError: undefined method 'shout' for "world":String

This raises a fascinating puzzle:

  • We already know that objects cannot hold methods. So :shout cannot live inside str1.
  • :shout cannot live inside String, because then str2 would also have access to it.

If objects cannot hold methods, and the class cannot hold this method, where on earth does shout live?

Ruby solves this by doing something brilliant: it quietly invents an invisible class on the fly.

The moment you define a method on str1, Ruby creates an anonymous, hidden class called an eigenclass (officially referred to as a singleton class).

Ruby then performs an architectural sleight of hand:

  1. It intercepts str1's internal klass pointer and repoints it to this new singleton class (#<Class:str1>).
  2. It sets the superclass of the singleton class to String.
  3. It places the :shout method inside the singleton class's method table.

When you call str1.shout, Ruby follows the klass pointer into #<Class:str1>, finds :shout, and runs it.

When you call str1.upcase, Ruby looks in #<Class:str1>, does not find :upcase, follows the superclass pointer up to String, finds :upcase, and runs it.

To regular code, the singleton class is almost completely transparent. You do not see it in str1.class (which still reports String). But you can prove it exists with Ruby's reflection methods:

str1.singleton_class
#=> #<Class:#<String:0x00007fffa80c2180>>

str1.singleton_methods
#=> [:shout]

"Class Methods" Do Not Exist

Once you understand eigenclasses, one of the biggest myths in Ruby evaporates: there is no such thing as a "class method".

Developers frequently write code like this:

class Post
  def self.recent
    # query recent posts
  end
end

Tutorials often say: "This defines a class method on Post."

In languages like Java or C++, a static method is a distinct language construct. But in Ruby, Post is not a special entity. Post is simply an object. It is an instance of the class Class.

Post.class
#=> Class

Because Post is an object, writing def Post.recent or def self.recent is doing the exact same thing as writing def str1.shout: it is defining a singleton method on an object.

The :recent method does not live in Post, and it does not live in Class. It lives in Post's own private eigenclass (#<Class:Post>).

In Ruby, there are only instance methods. What we call "class methods" are merely instance methods living on the singleton class of a class object. The entire language operates on one single, unified rule.

The Complete Method Lookup Ladder

When you type receiver.message, what is the exact order Ruby follows to find the code?

Ruby does not search haphazardly. It walks an exact, deterministic ladder called the ancestors chain. The first match it encounters executes immediately.

Here is the exact step-by-step lookup path:

  1. The Receiver's Eigenclass: If the object has any singleton methods, they get first priority.
  2. Prepended Modules on the Eigenclass: Any module added with prepend sits in front of the eigenclass.
  3. The Receiver's Class: The standard class where ordinary instance methods reside.
  4. Prepended Modules on the Class: If a module was prepended to the class, its methods override the class's own methods.
  5. Included Modules on the Class: If a module was included in the class, it is inserted directly above the class in the hierarchy.
  6. Superclasses (and their modules): Ruby climbs to the parent class, checking its prepends, own methods, and includes.
  7. Object, Kernel, and BasicObject: The root ancestors shared by virtually all Ruby objects.

What Happens When Nothing Matches?

If Ruby climbs all the way to BasicObject without finding a matching method, it does not immediately raise an error.

Instead, Ruby walks back down to the starting receiver and starts the entire search again from step one, this time searching for a method named method_missing.

Because Kernel provides a default implementation of method_missing that raises NoMethodError, your program only crashes if no intermediate module or class intercepts it.

This two-pass search is what powers Ruby's famous metaprogramming libraries, from ActiveRecord dynamic finders to OpenStruct.

How "Everything Is an Object" Runs Fast: Tagged Pointers

If every number, boolean, and nil value in Ruby is an object with methods, how does Ruby avoid grinding to a halt allocating heap memory for basic math?

If you run:

total = 0
1_000_000.times { |i| total += i }

Does Ruby allocate one million RObject structs on the heap?

In CRuby, the answer is no, thanks to an internal optimization called Tagged Pointers (Immediate Values).

On a 64-bit operating system, memory addresses are aligned to 8-byte boundaries. That means the lowest 3 bits of any valid heap pointer are always 000.

CRuby takes advantage of these unused bits. When a 64-bit value represents a small integer (called a Fixnum), Ruby shifts the integer left by one bit and sets the lowest bit to 1:

value = (integer << 1) | 1

When the Ruby virtual machine sees a value with the lowest bit set to 1, it knows: "This is not a heap pointer. This is the raw integer itself."

Similarly, CRuby reserves specific bit patterns for singleton values:

  • false is represented as 0x00
  • nil is represented as 0x08
  • true is represented as 0x14

When you call 42.even?, Ruby does not inspect a heap block. It detects the tagged pointer, looks up the method in the Integer class method table, and executes the code without a single byte of memory allocation or garbage collection overhead.

You get the clean conceptual purity of "everything is an object" combined with the efficiency of primitive register arithmetic.

The Mental Shift

Ruby's object model is often described as complex, but under the surface, it is remarkably minimal:

  1. Objects store state and an internal klass pointer. They never hold methods.
  2. Classes store methods and an internal super pointer. They never hold instance state.
  3. Singleton methods live in invisible eigenclasses, seamlessly spliced into the lookup chain.
  4. Class methods are just singleton methods on class objects, because classes are objects too.
  5. Tagged pointers preserve pure object semantics without sacrificing performance.

Once you see the object model through this lens, Ruby metaprogramming stops feeling like black magic. Concepts like class_eval, instance_eval, prepend, and singleton classes become predictable mechanical tools that follow one coherent set of rules.

When you first learned Ruby, what was the quirk in its object model that made you stop and rethink how programming languages work? And if you have used eigenclasses in production, what was the problem you solved with them?

References:

  • Ruby Core Documentation: Class and Object
  • Ruby Core Documentation: Object#singleton_class
  • Pat Shaughnessy: Ruby Under a Microscope (In-depth analysis of MRI C structures)
  • Paolo Perrotta: Metaprogramming Ruby 2 (The definitive guide to Ruby's object model)

articles.title: I Fixed WebGPU on Linux. Then Forgot How I Did It.

articles.body_html:
I spent a ridiculous amount of time trying to get WebGPU working properly on my Linux machine.

I eventually figured it out, wrote a script to launch Chrome with all the necessary flags, and even made a desktop launcher so I could just click an icon whenever I wanted to run browser-based AI models.

Problem solved.

Except recently, I started thinking about all the trouble I'd gone through and realized something.

I couldn't remember how I'd fixed it.

Actually, I couldn't even remember where I'd saved the script.

So I did what any reasonable developer would do in 2026. I sent an AI agent to search my computer for code I'd written myself.

And what did it find?

Not only had I saved the script, I'd also written documentation explaining how it worked and backed everything up in TWO different resource directories.

Apparently, past me was considerably more organized than present me remembered.

Anyway, since I've already done all the hard work (and then forgotten about it), I figured I might as well share what I learned.

I just wanted to run AI models in my browser

I've spent quite a bit of time experimenting with local AI models, particularly small language models running through Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime.

I love the idea of running models directly in the browser. No server to maintain, no API calls to pay for, and inference happens right on your own hardware.

WebGPU makes a lot of that possible by allowing web applications to use the GPU for computation.

Which sounds great, right?

Except my setup wasn't exactly cooperating.

I'm running Arch-based Linux with Wayland on a laptop with hybrid graphics:

  • Intel Raptor Lake UHD integrated graphics
  • NVIDIA RTX 4090 Laptop GPU

And getting Chrome, Vulkan, NVIDIA, and Wayland to play nicely together was an absolute pain.

There are several layers involved. Your GPU drivers need to work, Vulkan needs to find the right device, Chrome needs to use the right graphics backend, and WebGPU needs to initialize successfully.

And just because one of those things works doesn't mean the next one will.

I spent a lot of time troubleshooting different configurations before I finally had something reliable enough to use regularly.

The solution that worked for me

Eventually, I ended up with a Bash script that launches a separate Chrome instance configured specifically for WebGPU.

Here's the script I recovered:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Launch Google Chrome with NVIDIA PRIME offload + Vulkan + WebGPU on X11.
# Dedicated separate profile so it can run alongside normal Chrome.

set -euo pipefail

CHROME_PROFILE_DIR="${HOME}/.config/chrome-webgpu-nvidia"

mkdir -p "$CHROME_PROFILE_DIR"

VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT='*nvidia*' \
__NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1 \
__GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia \
__VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only \
google-chrome-stable \
  --user-data-dir="$CHROME_PROFILE_DIR" \
  --enable-unsafe-webgpu \
  --enable-features=Vulkan \
  --ozone-platform=x11 \
  "$@"

It's not particularly complicated to look at.

But getting to the point where I knew which settings to use was another story.

I also created a .desktop launcher for it, so now when I want to experiment with WebGPU, I can just open that version of Chrome without having to remember any of this.

Which, as we've established, is probably a good thing.

What all those settings actually do

1. Getting Chrome to use the NVIDIA GPU

My laptop has two GPUs. There's the integrated Intel GPU and the dedicated NVIDIA GPU.

With hybrid graphics, applications don't necessarily use the GPU you'd expect.

That's a problem when you're trying to run models on your RTX 4090 and your browser decides the integrated GPU looks perfectly adequate.

So my script sets four environment variables:

VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT='*nvidia*'
__NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1
__GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia
__VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only

Here's what they're for:

  • VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT filters the Vulkan driver manifests so that the NVIDIA driver is selected.
  • __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1 enables NVIDIA PRIME render offloading.
  • __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia selects NVIDIA for GLX vendor dispatch.
  • __VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only tells NVIDIA's Optimus Vulkan layer to expose only the NVIDIA GPU.

Not all four variables necessarily matter for every application or graphics path, but this combination was part of my working configuration.

The important thing was making sure Chrome could actually access and use the GPU I wanted.

2. Making Wayland cooperate by... not using native Wayland

This one still makes me laugh.

I'm running a Wayland desktop, but my working Chrome launcher includes:

--ozone-platform=x11

That tells Chrome to use its X11 backend, which runs through XWayland inside my Wayland session.

At the time, I was running into problems getting Vulkan and Chrome's native Wayland backend to cooperate with NVIDIA.

Running Chrome through XWayland was the workaround that finally worked for my setup.

So after all that effort to get things running properly under Wayland, part of my solution was essentially telling Chrome to pretend it was running under X11.

Sometimes the practical solution isn't the elegant one.

It's the one that actually works.

3. Giving Chrome its own profile

This was one of the more useful discoveries.

--user-data-dir="$CHROME_PROFILE_DIR"

Chrome normally reuses an existing browser instance when you try to launch it again with the same profile.

So if Chrome is already open and you try launching another window with different GPU flags, you might discover that your new settings aren't actually being applied.

Using a separate profile directory gives my WebGPU launcher its own Chrome process and GPU configuration.

That also means I can keep my regular browser open while running a separate instance for development.

No need to mess with my normal browsing setup every time I want to test something.

4. Enabling Vulkan and WebGPU

Finally, these two flags:

--enable-unsafe-webgpu
--enable-features=Vulkan

The first enables experimental WebGPU support and bypasses certain GPU restrictions.

The second enables Chromium's Vulkan graphics feature.

There's an important distinction here: enabling Vulkan in Chrome doesn't necessarily guarantee that WebGPU itself is using Vulkan through Dawn, Chromium's WebGPU implementation.

The exact behavior depends on your Chromium version, platform, and graphics configuration.

Also, --enable-unsafe-webgpu is intended for development and testing. It's not something I'd recommend casually enabling in your everyday browser.

A note about newer Chrome versions: WebGPU support on Linux has been improving, so you might not need this exact configuration anymore. In particular, newer releases have expanded support for Intel and NVIDIA hardware. Check your current browser and driver support before copying every flag into your own setup.

How to check whether it's actually working

After launching Chrome with the script, open:

chrome://gpu

Look at the Graphics Feature Status section.

Ideally, you want to see hardware acceleration enabled for WebGPU and Vulkan rather than software fallbacks.

It's also worth checking the GPU and driver information to make sure Chrome is using the NVIDIA device instead of Intel or a software renderer like SwiftShader.

But don't stop there.

Being able to see WebGPU listed as hardware accelerated doesn't guarantee your actual application will run correctly.

Try running a real WebGPU sample or the model you're planning to use.

I've learned this the hard way more than once.

For example, while building my recent Mimu note-taking app, Safari on my iPhone reported that WebGPU was available. But attempting to initialize the Whisper model with WebGPU caused the tab to crash and reload.

The WASM version worked fine.

And for that particular small model, WASM was fast enough that using WebGPU wasn't worth the trouble anyway.

That was another useful reminder that the theoretically faster option isn't always the best one.

And then I forgot where I put everything

So here's where this whole thing comes full circle.

Recently, I've started keeping detailed build logs for my projects.

Not just what I built, but what broke, what I tried, why I made certain decisions, and what I'd do differently if I approached the same problem again.

Writing more on DEV has actually encouraged this habit. Thinking about what I might eventually write makes me pay more attention to what I'm doing while I'm building.

And I've already found myself going back through my notes and reconsidering decisions I made just a day or two earlier.

Which got me thinking about all those earlier experiences with WebGPU.

I wished I'd documented them better.

Turns out, I had.

I just couldn't remember doing it.

My AI agent found the original launcher in:

~/.local/bin/chrome-webgpu-nvidia

The desktop entry was in:

~/.local/share/applications/

And the documentation and additional copies were sitting in my PINKPIXEL/RESOURCES directory.

In two different folders.

I had already done everything I was wishing past me had done.

I just hadn't done a particularly good job of making that information easy to find again.

Which is even funnier considering I'm currently building an app designed to help people capture, organize, and remember things.

Apparently, I really do need it.

What I learned from all this

The technical lesson here is that getting WebGPU working on Linux can involve more than just enabling a browser flag, especially with hybrid graphics.

Depending on your hardware and software versions, you may need to pay attention to which GPU is being selected, which graphics backend Chrome is using, and whether your application is actually getting hardware acceleration.

But I think the bigger lesson for me has less to do with WebGPU.

I've built a lot of things over the years. I've solved problems, experimented with technologies, and figured out workarounds that took far more effort than I expected.

And then I moved on to the next interesting thing.

I didn't always stop to think about what I'd learned or how useful that experience might be later.

That's something I've been trying to change.

Keeping build logs has made me more thoughtful about the decisions I'm making, and writing about my experiences has encouraged me to look at them more closely.

Sometimes that means discovering a better way to approach something.

Sometimes it means remembering a useful technique.

And sometimes it means finding out that I already solved a problem, documented it, backed it up twice, and completely forgot about the whole thing.

At least now I know where my WebGPU script is.

For the moment, anyway.

articles.title: My OSS Projects: dets
articles.description: This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or...
articles.body_html:
This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or helped to grow – with the back story, what they do well, where they struggle, and what's next. Previous parts: AngleSharp, MAGES, Piral, Electron.NET, Netpack and Picard.js.

We are getting close to the end of this series: only two projects left. Today's is one of the quieter ones – it has no logo that anyone remembers, no conference talk, and no hype. What it has is a job it does reliably: dets, a TypeScript declaration file bundler.

It started as a helper for Piral, and it grew up a bit since then.

What is dets?

dets generates a single .d.ts file from your TypeScript code. You tell it what the entry points are, and it produces one self-contained declaration file with only the API you care about – and no dependency on other declaration packages.

That's useful in two situations:

  1. You want to selectively expose an API (and not everything that happens to be exported somewhere).
  2. You want a self-contained declaration file that you can ship, copy, or publish as-is.

The package description says exactly this, in five words: "A TypeScript declaration file bundler". It's MIT licensed, lives at github.com/FlorianRappl/dets, and – to my own surprise – is downloaded several thousand times per week.

The back story: a shell for plugins

To explain why dets exists I have to explain how Piral thinks about the world.

In Piral, the app shell is a plugin-enhanced app: it loads micro frontends (pilets) at runtime and gives them an API to integrate with it – register a page, add an extension, access shared data, and so on. For micro frontend teams to be productive they need that shell on their machine: to debug locally, and to build and check their code against what the shell really offers.

And since the shell comes with an API, the natural thing (at least in the web world) is to ship TypeScript declarations for it. Then the IDE can tell you what is available, and your build tool can complain if your assumptions are wrong. (Compile errors are better than production errors. Always.)

"But the shell is written in TypeScript – don't we get that for free?"

That was my first thought, too. It is also wrong, for a few reasons:

  • The app shell is an application, not a library. Most of what's in there is not meant for micro frontends.
  • The API for the micro frontends is only a subset of the app shell.
  • The shell brings nothing of that API to the runtime. The types are compile-time only. There is no object you can point at and say "this is the API".

So what you'd need is a declaration file that describes just the part that is relevant. And that's something TypeScript's own tsc --declaration does not give you: it emits one declaration file per source file, mirrors your internal structure, and happily references everything.

The failed attempts

First I tried the obvious: take the plugin API definition of the app shell and feed it to the various type bundling tools out there. It did not go well. Whatever I tried either failed outright or produced vast amounts of ill-formatted garbage.

At some point you have to accept the pattern: type bundling – or type extraction in general – is not a solved problem.

One weekend, one experiment

That's when I spent a weekend on an experiment: Can I use the TypeScript compiler API to actually infer the types and re-build a .d.ts with only the API I care about?

It turns out: yes. But not easily.

Along the way I learned an awful lot about how TypeScript infers and enriches type information, and how its internal model is built up – symbols, declarations, types, flags, merging, aliases… you name it. Things that you never need to think about when writing TypeScript become very present when you try to print it.

The main catch, however, was the API itself. It was meant to be internal. At some point the TypeScript team wanted (and even tried out) a plugin story with real API users. But it seems they found it easier to leave it undocumented and keep it their safe space. Whoever uses the API should be prepared for surprises in future versions.

So dets became a tool that stands on an unstable foundation by design. That sounds worse than it is – it just means that keeping up with TypeScript versions is a feature of this project, not an accident (more on that below – including a look at what's inside).

Getting started

Install it as a dev dependency:

npm i dets --save-dev

(npx dets or a global install work, too.) Then point it at your entry module:

dets src/index.ts --name foo --files "src/**/*.ts" --out dist/index.d.ts

The options you will meet most often:

Option What it does
entry (positional) The entry-level modules to consume. This is what you should reach for in most cases.
--name The module name. If omitted, it's taken from the nearest package.json.
--files The files TypeScript gets to see.
--imports Packages whose imports should stay external (not bundled in).
--ignore Respect @ignore comments and drop those members (default: true).
--module-declaration Wrap the output in a declare module "name" { … } block (default: true).
--out The output path (default: ./dist/index.d.ts).

There are also lower-level options (--types, --apis) for selecting types by file and interfaces by InterfaceName:FilePath – handy when the API is defined as an interface, but not exported from a single entry point (hello, app shells).

From code

If you want to integrate dets into your own tooling, there is a programmatic API, too:

import { generateDeclaration } from 'dets';
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';

const content = await generateDeclaration({
  name: 'my-app-shell',
  root: process.cwd(),
  files: ['src/**/*.ts'],
  types: ['src/api.ts'],
});

writeFileSync('dist/index.d.ts', content);

generateDeclaration returns the content; writing it somewhere is up to you. (If you need finer control, setupVisitorContext, fillVisitorContextFromApi and fillVisitorContextFromTypes give you the building blocks – e.g. to say "use this exported object as the API".)

Shaping the output

Bundling everything that is reachable is the easy part. The interesting part is controlling what ends up in the file.

Special comments

dets understands a few comment tags:

export interface Foo {
  bar: string;
  /**
   * Internal – should not be visible for consumers.
   * @ignore
   */
  secret: number;
}
  • @ignore drops the member from the output (can be disabled via --no-ignore).
  • @dets_preserve keeps an @ignored member and removes only the tag itself – useful if something is hidden in one context but needed in another.
  • @dets_removeprop and @dets_removeclause are for merged interfaces: they remove named properties or extends clauses from the combination. (Declaration merging is a powerful TypeScript feature, and a splendid source of surprises.)

Plugins

For everything else there are plugins. They hook into the phases shown above (before-init, before-process, after-process, before-stringify) and can modify the model before it is printed. There are two styles: a classic one – an object with type, name and run(context) – and a modern one, where a single plugin implements multiple lifecycle hooks:

const plugin = {
  name: 'my-plugin',
  'before-init'(context) {
    // prepare something
  },
  'after-process'(context) {
    // adjust the collected types
  },
};

There is also a built-in createExcludePlugin(['some-module']) to drop whole modules from the output (declaration merges on other modules still apply).

Under the hood: the TypeScript compiler API

Time to open the hood. If you have never touched the compiler API, here's the mental model that made everything click for me.

Three layers: text, syntax, meaning

When TypeScript processes your code, it builds up information in layers:

  1. The parser turns text into a tree of nodes – the AST. A node knows what is written and where (ClassDeclaration, Parameter, StringKeyword, …). That's purely syntactic. A node has no idea what Foo in x: Foo actually is.
  2. The binder walks the tree and creates symbols. A symbol is the semantic identity behind a name: "there is a class called SomeClass, with the members value and foo". Symbols point back to their declarations (the nodes). And here is the key trick: multiple declarations can share one symbol. That's how declaration merging works – an interface and a class with the same name, two interfaces in two files, a namespace that extends a function. In the AST these are unrelated nodes; in the symbol table they are one thing.
  3. The checker computes types from symbols and nodes – lazily, on demand, and cached. It resolves imports and aliases, follows export { a as b }, and infers what nobody wrote down.

This second part – symbols and types – is what I mean by the "semantic tree" that sits next to the AST. It is why TypeScript can do what it does: completions, refactorings, error messages, and .d.ts emit all depend on it. The syntax alone is not enough: export * from './foo' tells you nothing about what is exported until something resolves ./foo, finds its symbols, and merges them in.

Nodes vs. symbols vs. type nodes vs. types

The naming is confusing, so let's pin it down using a class from dets' own test fixtures:

  • Node (ts.Node): one piece of syntax. Everything you can point at in the source.
  • Type node (ts.TypeNode): a node that is a type annotation – string, Foo<T>, A | B, { x: number }. It is syntax: it exists only if someone wrote it. [1, 2] has no type node, but it very much has a type.
  • Symbol (ts.Symbol): the named entity the binder created. Carries flags (Class, Interface, Alias, …), its declarations, and its members / exports.
  • Type (ts.Type): what the checker knows. foo() above returns string, even though that's written nowhere.

The reason this matters for dets: the output is syntax. A .d.ts is text, so we need type nodes to print – but for inferred things, the checker only gives us types. The bridge is checker.typeToTypeNode(type), which converts semantics back into syntax. That one function is the reason dets works at all for code like foo() { return this.value; }.

A tiny example of the three APIs working together (this is not dets code, just the shape of things):

import ts from 'typescript';

const program = ts.createProgram(['src/index.ts'], { strict: true });
const checker = program.getTypeChecker();
const file = program.getSourceFile('src/index.ts')!;

ts.forEachChild(file, (node) => {
  if (ts.isClassDeclaration(node) && node.name) {
    // syntax: what is written
    console.log(ts.SyntaxKind[node.kind]); // "ClassDeclaration"

    // meaning: the symbol behind the name
    const symbol = checker.getSymbolAtLocation(node.name)!;
    console.log(symbol.declarations?.length); // 2+ if merged

    // knowledge: the type (and back to a printable type node)
    const type = checker.getTypeAtLocation(node);
    const typeNode = checker.typeToTypeNode(type, undefined, ts.NodeBuilderFlags.NoTruncation);
  }
});

From options to program

Where does the program come from? In dets, generateDeclaration (in src/commands.ts) is the conductor. Roughly:

  1. Collect the source files (files, the files of the apis, and the types entries – minus whatever is excluded).
  2. Create a ts.Program with a small, fixed set of compiler options: JS allowed, esModuleInterop, ESNext modules, React JSX – and Bundler module resolution if the installed TypeScript is 5.3 or newer, Node10 otherwise. (That's the "keeping up with TypeScript versions" part, in one line.)
  3. Fill a visitor context with the exports that should be part of the result – from an exported object (apis) or from all exports of a module (types).
  4. Run the plugin phases around the visitor: before-init → create the visitor → before-process → processQueue() → after-process → before-stringify.
  5. Stringify the result into the final declaration.

Everything interesting happens in step 4.

The most important file: src/input/node.ts

If dets has a heart, it is src/input/node.ts. It contains the DeclVisitor: the class that walks declarations and converts them into an intermediate model (plain objects describing interfaces, classes, aliases, functions, …) that the output stage can print.

A work queue, not a recursive walk

The visitor starts with the exports from the context and puts them in a queue. processQueue drains the queue; every declaration goes through processNode, which is basically a big dispatcher:

// simplified
processNode(node: ts.Node) {
  this.processed.push(node); // remember first, handle later

  if (ts.isTypeAliasDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getAlias(node));
  } else if (ts.isFunctionDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getFunctionDeclaration(node));
  } else if (ts.isInterfaceDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeExportedInterface(node);
  } else if (ts.isClassDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getClass(node));
  } else if (ts.isEnumDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getEnum(node));
  } else if (ts.isExportDeclaration(node)) {
    // export { a as b }   vs.   export * from './x'
  } else {
    this.printWarning('type', node); // we don't know this one (yet)
  }
}

The key design decision: a reference is a name, not a body. When a type mentions another type (foo: Bar), the visitor does not descend into Bar right there. It enqueues the declaration of Bar and puts a reference-by-name into the model. That has two nice consequences:

  • Every declaration is emitted exactly once, no matter how often it's referenced.
  • Cyclic types (A references B, B references A) terminate for free.

That is also how "tree shaking" for types works: if nobody references it from the entry, it never gets into the queue.

Walk the nodes, ask the checker only when needed

Most of the file is getTypeNode: a long chain of ts.isX guards that routes each type node to a handler – unions, literals, arrays, type references, indexed access, keyof/readonly, mapped types, conditional types, function and constructor types, infer, intersections, tuples (and named/optional/rest members), typeof queries, template literal types, and imports. Keywords like string or unknown are handled as constants.

Interestingly, the file does not switch on ts.Type flags. dets mostly walks the syntax and only reaches for the checker when the syntax doesn't say enough. The typical case is a missing annotation:

// simplified
getReturnType(node: ts.SignatureDeclaration) {
  if (node.type) {
    return this.getTypeNode(node.type); // written down – just use it
  }

  // not written down: ask the checker what it inferred
  const signature = this.checker.getSignatureFromDeclaration(node);
  const returnType = this.checker.getReturnTypeOfSignature(signature);
  const typeNode = this.checker.typeToTypeNode(returnType, undefined, ts.NodeBuilderFlags.NoTruncation);
  return this.getTypeNode(typeNode);
}

(NoTruncation is important – by default TypeScript abbreviates large types with ..., which is great for hover tooltips and terrible for a declaration file.)

The same pattern shows up for variables (annotation, then initializer, then inferred type), default exports, and typeof queries on imported values, which are expanded into synthetic interfaces.

Where symbols come in: merging, aliases, names

Symbols earn their keep in three places.

Declaration merging. When dets handles an interface, it asks the checker for the type's symbol and collects all interface declarations of that symbol – skipping those that come from imported packages. Heritage clauses, members and type parameters of all declarations are combined (without duplicates) into one interface. Classes do the same with interfaces that share the class symbol. That's the scenario where @dets_removeprop and @dets_removeclause come in handy.

Export aliases. For export { a as b }, the visitor resolves the specifier to the actual symbol (getExportSpecifierLocalTargetSymbol, getAliasedSymbol) and then renames the result.

Names. Two different declarations may have the same name – from different files, or an import that collides with a local type. All declarations of one symbol share one name, and a collision gets a ___N suffix:

// simplified
createName(name: string) {
  const prefix = `${name}___`;
  const taken = new Set([...this.names.values()].filter((n) => n === name || n.startsWith(prefix)));
  return taken.size > 0 ? `${prefix}${taken.size}` : name;
}

Yes, a type called Foo___1 in your declaration file is slightly ugly. It is also correct, which beats the alternative.

Externals

Not everything should be bundled in. If a type comes from an external package, it's not copied: includeInContext checks whether the symbol belongs to a package (via a helper called getPackage), and if so, it becomes an import instead of part of the model. That's what the --imports option controls.

When it doesn't know

Whatever the visitor does not understand ends up in a warning (Could not resolve type at position …) rather than a crash. The log levels (0.8.0) let you decide how loud that should be. When you see such a warning on your code: that's a new test case waiting to happen.

How testing works in dets

A tool whose job is to produce exact text from arbitrary code has a natural test strategy: feed it small pieces of code and compare the output to the expected text.

The setup is refreshingly boring:

  • Fixtures. tests/assets/ contains ~150 small TypeScript files: class1.ts, interface1.ts, merge1.ts, enum1.ts, react1.tsx, vue1.ts, … Each one isolates a single feature or bug.
  • A helper. runTestFor(name, options) calls the real generateDeclaration with sensible defaults: module name test, the assets folder as root, and the fixture as both files and types. Options can be overridden per test.
  • Tests. About 30 test files (classes.test.ts, merge.test.ts, tuple.test.ts, typeof.test.ts, …), run with Vitest. Each test runs the helper on a fixture and compares the result to a template literal.

Here is what the simplest one looks like. The fixture:

export class SomeClass {
  public constructor(private value: string) {}

  foo() {
    return this.value;
  }
}

And the test – abbreviated (the repo has the exact expected text), with the expectation being the full text of the generated declaration:

import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { runTestFor } from './helper';

test('should be able to handle exported classes with constructor', async () => {
  const result = await runTestFor('class1.ts');
  expect(result).toBe(`declare module "test" {
  export class SomeClass {
    private value;
    public constructor(value: string);
    foo(): string;
  }
}
`);
});

Note the foo(): string; – that is the inferred return type from the checker, making a round trip through typeToTypeNode.

A few things I like about this approach:

  • It's a real end-to-end test. No mocking of the compiler. Every test creates an actual program and uses the actual checker – which is exactly where the bugs live.
  • Exact comparison (toBe). No normalization of whitespace. The declaration file is a product; indentation and order are part of it.
  • Every bug gets a fixture. Titles like "should treat readonly fields correctly (issue 55)" are a diary of the project. The 14 tests in classes.test.ts alone cover constructors, modifiers, generics (explicit and implicit), implemented interfaces, React classes from externals and bundled in, static members, accessors, readonly, and class/interface merging.
  • Real-world typings. The helper can also point at the typings of piral-base and piral-core (the original use case!), and the dev dependencies read like a who's who of typings: React, Redux, React Router, styled-components, Vue. If it can handle those, it can handle your code.

The CI (GitHub Actions) runs the tests and the build on every push to main or develop and for pull requests to develop. A push to develop publishes a pre-release to npm under the next tag (with the run number in the version); a push to main publishes the real thing – with provenance – and creates the git tag. The build script even runs dets on itself: the shipped dist/index.d.ts is bundled by dets, with typescript as the external import. If the tool can't describe its own API, that's a red flag.

One more detail from the changelog: in 0.16.5 the tests moved from Jest to Vitest – a good reminder that even a test suite is just another dependency to keep alive.

The changelog: a tour of 1.0

With about 60 changelog entries, the CHANGELOG tells the story better than I could. I find it easiest to read in four themes.

Teaching it the language

The early releases are a march through the language: 0.1 brought classes, generics and constructor calls (and extends/implements came in 0.1.5). 0.2.0 was the big one: a rewrite of the engine for better resolution and accuracy, with support for dynamically placed imports and destructuring. 0.3.0 added interface merging resolution, tuples and enums, 0.3.2 accessors (get/set) and readonly. Later highlights: overloads and the satisfies operator (0.12), named tuples (0.11.2, 0.12.3), triple-slash directives (0.14.1), the spread operator (0.16.3), and in 1.0.0 optional tuple entries.

Control

Once the output was right, people wanted to shape it. 0.8.0 added log levels with custom log providers. 0.9.0 introduced @ignore handling and the @dets_preserve, @dets_removeprop and @dets_removeclause tags. 0.10.0 added lifecycle plugins (and declaration merging for externals). 0.12.0 added the module-declaration option, 0.14.0 a modern plugin API with multiple lifecycle hooks (and made the API async), and 0.18.0 the excluded option.

Keeping up with TypeScript

The thread that runs through the whole history. TypeScript became a peer dependency in 0.4.0, 0.7.0 added TypeScript 4, 0.11.0 added guards for older versions, 0.13.0 added TypeScript 5 and dropped TypeScript 3, and 0.14.1 fixed TypeScript 5.3 not considering externals. 1.0.0 finally improved the version independence – and fixed importing types from hidden submodules.

Housekeeping

Bundling moved from ncc to esbuild (0.13.0), Node 14, 16 and 18 were dropped step by step (0.15, 0.17, 0.18) – the minimum is Node.js 20 – the tests moved to Vitest (0.16.5), and publishing now uses npm's trusted publishing via GitHub Actions (0.18.0). Plus a long tail of "fixed X" entries, many triggered by issue reports: dots in names (0.16.5, thanks to @longlostbro), readonly in constructors (0.17.0), and more.

And then, finally, 1.0.0: the version number that says "this has been around long enough".

Where dets shines

  • API subsets. Exactly the use case from above: take a big application, expose only the part that's meant for others.
  • One file. Combining all the .d.ts files of a library into a single one – especially if the library is bundled and compressed anyway. It's tidy.
  • Controllable. Special comments, plugins and a programmatic API let you adjust the result without post-processing strings.
  • TypeScript-version independent. Over the years it moved from TypeScript 3 through 4 to 5 and the 1.0.0 release improved version independence further.

Where dets struggles

Let's be honest:

  • It stands on internals. I use TypeScript's compiler API – the part that's intentionally under-documented and not stable. A TypeScript release can (and sometimes does) break things. The changelog is full of entries like "fix for TypeScript 5.3" for exactly this reason.
  • Type extraction is hard. Complex type-level programming, odd declaration merging, and exotic constructs may need a plugin or a comment hint to come out right.
  • Small project. There are a few dozen stars and a small group of users. It does one thing, and there's not much of a community around it.
  • Documentation. The README covers the options, but it is not a book. For the more advanced scenarios the best documentation is the source and the tests.

dets today

In the Piral world, dets is used in two places:

  • For the emulator typings of Piral: the app shell's API is turned into a declaration file that ships with the emulator, so micro frontend developers get completion and type checks locally.
  • For libraries in the ecosystem: combining all the .d.ts files into one – the nicest fit for libraries that are bundled / compressed anyway.

Beyond that, the npm download counter shows about 7,000 downloads per week (12–18 October 2026: 7,215) – more than I'd have guessed for a tool that started as an internal helper.

What's next: TypeScript 7

The big question mark: TypeScript 7. The compiler is being ported to a native implementation, and with that, the future of the TypeScript API as we know it is still to be determined. I am sure that an API will return at some point – too many tools depend on it, and it would be strange to not offer a way to build on top of the compiler.

Until then, the plan is simple: we stay with TypeScript 6 (or 5) and are happy to keep on bundling. If dets needs an adaptation once the new API shapes up, I'll make it – and write about it, probably.

One more project to go after this one – and it's a big one. Stay tuned!

articles.description: On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped an emergency security release for two critical vulnerabilities in...
articles.body_html:
On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped an emergency security release for two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself. The pair is being called PHP2Shell:

  • CVE-2026-109618
  • CVE-2026-109619

Both have a 9.2 Critical CVSS score. Both can expose vulnerable PHP services to unauthenticated remote code execution and memory disclosure. And neither one is fixed by updating Laravel, WordPress, Symfony, a Composer package, or your application code.

This is the important part:

The vulnerable thing is the PHP interpreter that runs your application.

So yes, the meme is funny. The patch window is not.

First: should you be worried?

You should move this to the top of the queue if you run PHP on an internet-facing service and your runtime is any version from PHP 5.4 through PHP 8.5.11.

That includes more than the obvious php-fpm server in a VM:

  • PHP-FPM behind Nginx or Apache
  • Apache mod_php
  • WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Moodle, and other PHP-based products
  • Docker images built from php:* base images
  • Kubernetes workloads
  • queue workers and scheduled jobs
  • application images deployed to Cloud Run, ECS, App Engine Flexible, or similar platforms
  • vendor software that silently bundles its own PHP runtime

This is why security incidents around language runtimes are awkward: everyone knows where the repository is, but fewer teams can answer which PHP binary is actually serving production traffic right now?

What actually happened?

PHP receives a request, allocates memory, builds internal structures, runs your code, cleans everything up, and does it again for the next request. Most of the time, none of this is visible to an application developer. It should not be visible.

PHP2Shell lives in the parts of that lifecycle you only notice when something has already gone wrong: out-of-memory handling, cleanup, freed memory, and reused workers.

Think of a restaurant kitchen.

Normally, an order comes in, a tray is prepared, food is served, the tray is cleaned, and the next order starts with an empty tray. These vulnerabilities are different flavours of the kitchen being interrupted mid-cleanup—and the next order being served from a tray the system thought was safe, but was not.

That is a deliberately simplified analogy. The practical consequence is not: “your page crashes.” The reported impact is much worse: an unauthenticated attacker may be able to manipulate the runtime into leaking memory or executing code in the PHP process.

The two CVEs, in human language

CVE The technical shape The plain-English version Why defenders care
CVE-2026-109618 During an out-of-memory condition, PHP can be interrupted while request data is only partially initialized. Subsequent cleanup can treat that invalid state as valid. The runtime gets interrupted while setting up the request, then later cleans up a half-built object as if it were complete. The failure path can become an attacker-controlled path.
CVE-2026-109619 Request-owned state can remain reachable after its backing memory has been freed. A later request on the same worker can use stale state before normal initialization resets it. One request leaves behind a poisonous sticky note; the next request on the same worker reads it before the desk is reset. Long-lived, reused PHP workers make cross-request state especially relevant.

The research and vendor advisories use precise memory-management language because the details matter for exploitability. You do not need to reproduce that research to respond safely. The operational conclusion is already clear: update the runtime, restart/redeploy every worker that might still have the old binary or old in-memory state, and verify the version that is actually live.

Why “we use a framework” is not the answer

Framework updates are valuable. They just solve a different class of problem.

A typical framework vulnerability might be triggered by a route, a package feature, an insecure deserialization path, or an app-level configuration choice. With PHP2Shell, the issue is underneath that stack:

Your application
↓
Laravel / WordPress / Symfony / custom code
↓
Composer dependencies
↓
PHP runtime   ← the vulnerable layer
↓
OS or container image

You can have pristine dependencies, a clean SAST report, and still be running an affected PHP interpreter. That is why the right opening question is not “Which repo uses PHP?” It is “Which live workloads execute PHP?”

Which versions are affected—and what fixes them?

The disclosed affected range is PHP 5.4 through PHP 8.5.11.

The initial fixed upstream releases are:

Supported branch Fixed release
PHP 8.5 8.5.12
PHP 8.4 8.4.27
PHP 8.3 8.3.36
PHP 8.2 8.2.35

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life and are not receiving an upstream fix. If you are on one of those branches, the decision is not “which patch do we wait for?” It is “which supported PHP branch can we upgrade to safely and quickly?”

One nuance for distro users: a Linux distribution can backport a security patch while retaining a different-looking upstream version string. Follow your distribution’s security advisory and package changelog, then verify the installed package. For custom builds and official PHP images, move to a fixed upstream release.

The container trap: patching the host may change nothing

This is the moment where many incident checklists quietly fail.

Imagine a host running the latest system PHP package. Great. But your production app is deployed as this:

FROM php:8.3-fpm
COPY . /var/www/html

The PHP process serving requests came from the image, not from the host package manager. Updating the host does not alter the PHP binary already baked into that image.

The real fix path is:

update base image or PHP package
→ rebuild image
→ push a new immutable digest
→ redeploy every workload
→ verify the running container

The same rule applies to queue workers, cron jobs, admin jobs, and one-off worker deployments. They often have a separate Dockerfile, release pipeline, or autoscaling pool.

“The build succeeded” is not the final check. “The running workload uses the patched runtime” is.

A calm, practical response plan

1. Find every runtime

Start by checking what a machine or container is running:

php -v
php --ini

For container fleets, find images that contain PHP, then inspect the deployed digest in your orchestration platform. Search your CI definitions too: the old base image may be pinned in a reusable workflow rather than in the application repository.

Do not forget:

  • background queues
  • scheduled jobs
  • worker pools
  • maintenance scripts
  • staging and pre-production environments that hold production-like data
  • marketplace or vendor products with bundled PHP

2. Patch the runtime

Update to the fixed release for your supported branch—or to a vendor-confirmed package that contains the backported fix. For source builds, use the fixed upstream release. For containers, rebuild from a fixed base image or package set.

3. Restart or redeploy the processes

Installing a package is only half a fix if PHP-FPM or Apache is still running an old process in memory. Restart the relevant service. In container platforms, deploy fresh tasks/pods/instances from the patched image.

This matters especially for a bug involving request-owned state and reused workers: stale, running processes are not where you want to gamble on “probably fine.”

4. Verify the live environment

Check the runtime version from a newly started process, not just from your laptop or CI log:

php -v

For containers, also verify the new image digest is the one your deployment actually pulled. An autoscaler can keep old replicas alive longer than expected; an image tag can be reused; a rollout can partially fail. Those are normal operational problems. They are also how a completed patch turns into an incomplete remediation.

5. Monitor and investigate, without turning this into panic theatre

The FBI’s public guidance recommends prioritizing internet-facing systems, watching for suspicious PHP processes launching command shells or downloading files, and preserving relevant logs if compromise indicators appear. Qualys also reported that Cloudflare had observed attack traffic, which is a good reason to treat external exposure as urgent rather than theoretical.

Useful places to review:

  • web-server access and error logs
  • PHP-FPM / Apache error logs
  • process-execution telemetry from affected hosts and containers
  • WAF and load-balancer events
  • application error-rate and restart telemetry
  • image-scanner results after the rebuild

Unexpected 5xx spikes, repeated process crashes, large unusual request bodies, unexpected shell processes, or unexplained downloads deserve incident-response attention. They are signals to investigate—not proof by themselves that the CVE was exploited.

“Can a WAF save us?”

A WAF can buy time. It cannot patch a vulnerable interpreter.

Cloud guidance for this incident recommends using managed WAF protections and being careful about oversized request bodies while patching. That is reasonable defence in depth, especially for public applications. Roll new rules out in preview/canary mode where feasible, look for application-specific false positives, then enforce them.

But do not let a temporary rule become a reason to defer the update. A rule protects only the traffic it sees, only the shapes it recognizes, and only the applications placed behind it. The runtime update is the remediation.

The posts people are sharing on X

These are real posts published after the disclosure. They are included here because they add useful operational perspective—not because social media is a source of truth. The PHP security advisory and your platform/vendor guidance should drive the actual patch plan.

FBI Cyber Division: treat exposed installations as urgent

Qualys: patch, restart workers, and verify the runtime

Datadog: check versions across the organization

The things teams will get wrong this week

“We updated WordPress, so we are safe.”

Maybe you are safer from a WordPress vulnerability. That is not the same as replacing the PHP binary that runs WordPress.

“We upgraded the server package.”

Excellent—unless the service runs inside a container, an immutable image, a separate worker pool, or a vendor distribution with its own runtime.

“Our scanner says the repository is clean.”

Source scanning does not prove the running infrastructure has the right runtime. Scan the image, check the deployed digest, and verify the live process.

“We are on PHP 8.1, but it is stable.”

Stable is not supported. There is no upstream security release for PHP 8.1 or older here. Upgrade planning just became incident response work.

“We put a WAF rule in front of it.”

Good temporary mitigation. Still not a patch.

Your incident checklist

  • [ ] Identify every production, worker, and scheduled workload that executes PHP.
  • [ ] Confirm whether its PHP runtime is in the affected range.
  • [ ] Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35, or a vendor-confirmed patched build.
  • [ ] Upgrade PHP 8.1 and older to a supported branch.
  • [ ] Rebuild custom images without relying on a stale cache.
  • [ ] Redeploy every workload and restart long-lived PHP processes.
  • [ ] Verify the live runtime version and image digest.
  • [ ] Apply temporary WAF/edge controls while rollout completes.
  • [ ] Review security telemetry and preserve evidence if compromise indicators appear.
  • [ ] Record which environments are verified and which still need work.

The takeaway

PHP is a widely deployed runtime having a serious emergency patch day.

The less funny takeaway is that runtime upgrades cannot live forever in a low-priority maintenance bucket. The moment a core vulnerability lands, the teams that respond well are the ones that already know:

  1. where their runtimes are,
  2. how their images are built,
  3. how to roll out a change everywhere, and
  4. how to prove that the change reached production.

Patch it. Redeploy it. Verify it.

References

  • PHP’s October 21 security announcement
  • PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109618
  • PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109619
  • Google Cloud’s remediation guidance

Have you checked your worker images yet, or only the web servers?
