articles.title: The Hidden Bugs Behind Duplicate API Requests
articles.description: One click on "Place order." Two rows in the orders table, created 40 milliseconds apart, identical...
articles.body_html:
One click on "Place order." Two rows in the orders table, created 40 milliseconds apart, identical down to the last field.

Nothing in the frontend code looks wrong. The server logs show two requests, both returning 201. Whoever wrote the endpoint is fairly sure it only creates one order per call, and they're right. It was called twice.

"Duplicate request" is a symptom with at least six different causes, and the fixes don't overlap much. Some of these causes are harmless (React in development), some are annoying (a double-clicked button), and one is genuinely dangerous: a client that timed out and sent the request again, while the server had already done the work. This article goes through them roughly in the order I'd check them, and spends the most time on that last one, because it's the one that costs money.

Before you debug: is it really a duplicate?

Three things look like duplicates and aren't.

CORS preflight. A cross-origin request with a JSON Content-Type, an Authorization header, or a method like PUT makes the browser send an OPTIONS request first. In DevTools the URL appears twice. Look at the Method column. (MDN: CORS preflight)

Development-only behavior. If the doubles show up on your machine but not in production, go straight to the React section below.

A different caller. A service worker, browser extension, or second tab can send requests that resemble yours. The Initiator column in the Network tab points at the line that started each request.

Then do the single most useful thing: log a request ID on the server. One request on the server means you're misreading the client. Two means keep reading.

React runs your effect twice (on purpose) 

function Product({ id }) {
  const [product, setProduct] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/products/${id}`)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(setProduct);
  }, [id]);
}

Under <StrictMode> in development, this sends two requests on mount. In a production build it sends one.

That's deliberate. With Strict Mode on, React runs an extra setup, cleanup, setup cycle on each effect in development, to expose effects that don't clean up after themselves. The behavior arrived with React 18, and the surprise it caused is well documented in facebook/react #24502, where users asked for it to be explained better in the docs.

Removing Strict Mode makes the symptom disappear and leaves the bug. If an effect misbehaves when it runs twice, it will also misbehave when a user navigates away and back.

For reads, add a cleanup that cancels the request:

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  fetch(`/api/products/${id}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setProduct)
    .catch(err => {
      if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setError(err);
    });

  return () => controller.abort();
}, [id]);

You'll still see two requests in the Network tab in development, but the first is cancelled and only the second can touch state. An AbortController is better than the common ignore flag here: as this DEV Community post points out, the flag discards the result but still lets the first request download its whole response.

Cancelling on the client does not undo anything the server already did. Which brings up the real question this section raises: what is the effect doing? A duplicate GET is noise. A duplicate POST fired from an effect means a non-idempotent action is tied to rendering. React's guidance is that effects exist to synchronize with external systems, and that you don't need an effect to handle a user event. Creating an order belongs in the click handler, where it runs once per click.

Race conditions: the stale response wins

Sometimes two different requests are in flight and the older one finishes last.

A search box fires on every keystroke. The user types "re", then "react". The request for "re" is slow, the one for "react" is quick. Results for "react" render, then results for "re" arrive and overwrite them. The page now shows results for a query that no longer matches the input.

Nothing was sent twice, and nothing here is React-specific. The UI depends on the order responses arrive instead of the order the user acted. The cleanup shown above fixes it, since React runs the previous effect's cleanup before the next effect. If you'd rather not cancel, the flag version works too:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(data => { if (!ignore) setResults(data); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [query]);

Debouncing the input reduces how many requests you send. The cleanup makes sure the right one wins. They solve different problems, and a search box usually needs both.

The double click

A checkout button, an 800 ms API call, and a user who isn't sure the first click registered.

Disabling the button during submission is the obvious fix, with one catch. State updates don't apply synchronously inside the handler that sets them, so two clicks that land before React re-renders can both pass an if (submitting) check. A ref closes that gap:

function CheckoutButton() {
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const inFlight = useRef(false);

  async function handleClick() {
    if (inFlight.current) return;   // the real lock
    inFlight.current = true;
    setSubmitting(true);            // the visual feedback
    try {
      await placeOrder();
    } finally {
      inFlight.current = false;
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick} disabled={submitting}>
      {submitting ? 'Placing order…' : 'Place order'}
    </button>
  );
}

This protects one component in one tab. A second tab, a mobile app, or a retry after a dropped connection walks right past it. Treat it as UI feedback, and keep the safety check on the server.

The same handler attached twice

If the server log shows two identical requests a few milliseconds apart and the button logic is fine, count the listeners.

// runs on every route change
function init() {
  document.querySelector('#save')
    .addEventListener('click', () => saveDraft());
}

addEventListener ignores a repeat registration only when the function reference and capture flag are the same. An inline arrow function is a new object every call, so after three route changes one click runs saveDraft() three times. (MDN: addEventListener)

The usual sources are SPA code that attaches listeners imperatively on every navigation, jQuery's .on() inside a function that runs on every partial render, and React effects that subscribe without returning a cleanup. A form with both onSubmit on the <form> and onClick on its submit button doing the same job produces the same symptom.

In Chrome DevTools, select the element and open the Event Listeners panel. Two click entries where you expected one is your answer.

Retries: duplicates made by code that's trying to help

This is the case worth slowing down for.

You send a POST /orders. Ten seconds pass. Your client times out. Here is everything you know at that moment: you did not receive a response. Here is what you don't know:

  1. The request never reached the server.
  2. The server processed it, and the response was lost on the way back.
  3. The server is still working on it.

From the client these three look identical. If you retry in case 2 or 3, the operation runs twice.

HTTP has vocabulary for this. RFC 9110, section 9.2.2 defines idempotent methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE, where repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. POST isn't in that set, and neither is PATCH in general. The RFC's error-handling section also notes that some requests can be automatically retried after a connection failure, pointing to section 9.2.2 for which ones. Secondary write-ups summarize the rule as: don't automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless you know it's effectively idempotent or can tell the original was never applied (ApyHub, a DEV Community post on safe failover).

Check what your client library does by default

Retry behavior varies by library and version, so read your client's documentation instead of assuming. One public example: a GitLab client-library change (merge request 2945) added an option to restrict retries to idempotent methods, because its default check retried any method on a 5xx response, which could duplicate a side effect the server had already applied. That's one project's default, but it shows how the problem hides: nobody wrote a retry for POST /orders; a generic retry policy did.

Retries multiply across layers

If the browser code retries 3 times, the API gateway retries 3 times, and the service retries its database call 3 times, one click can become 27 attempts at the bottom. Amazon's Builders' Library article on timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter makes this point about stacked retries, and also calls retries "selfish": each one spends more of the server's time to improve the caller's odds. Its recommendations are timeouts based on downstream latency, capped exponential backoff, jitter so clients don't all retry in lockstep, and limiting retries (the AWS SDK has used a token bucket for this since 2016).

Infrastructure retries too. Reverse proxies can pass a failed request to another upstream. For example, nginx's proxy_next_upstream documents that non-idempotent requests aren't passed on by default unless you opt in with non_idempotent. Read the equivalent setting for whatever sits in front of your app, and check access logs on every hop.

A retry helper that actually retries HTTP failures

One trap when writing your own: fetch() resolves successfully even when the server answers 503. A try/catch around it never sees the failure. You have to look at the status yourself.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(res) {
    super(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    this.status = res.status;
  }
}

const RETRYABLE_STATUS = new Set([408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);

function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') return false;
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return RETRYABLE_STATUS.has(err.status);
  return err instanceof TypeError; // fetch rejects with TypeError on network failure
}

async function withRetry(fn, { retries = 4, baseMs = 200, capMs = 5000 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt >= retries || !isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
      const delay = Math.random() * ceiling;          // full jitter
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, delay));
    }
  }
}

// usage
const res = await withRetry(async () => {
  const r = await fetch('/api/orders', { method: 'POST', /* ... */ });
  if (!r.ok) throw new HttpError(r);
  return r;
});

I ran this helper against a stub that returns 503 twice and then 201: it made three attempts and returned the 201. A 400 was thrown after one attempt, as intended. A production version should also honor a Retry-After header when the server sends one.

Retrying a POST with this helper is only safe if the server can recognize the repeat. That's the next section.

Making the server safe to call twice

Everything above reduces how often a duplicate arrives. None of it can remove the three-way ambiguity after a timeout, because the network is allowed to lose a response. For operations that must not happen twice, the main defense is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation, the server records it with the result, and a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.

Stripe's API is the best-known example. Their documentation says the idempotency layer saves the status code and body of the first request for a key, whether it succeeded or failed, and returns that for later requests with the same key. Keys can be up to 255 characters, and reusing a key with different parameters produces an error. GET and DELETE don't take keys because they're idempotent by definition.

There's also a standards effort: the IETF HTTPAPI working group's Idempotency-Key HTTP header field draft. As of the version I read (draft-07, October 2025), it's an active Internet-Draft, not an RFC, so details may change.

Client: create the key once, reuse it on every retry 

// Create it when the user's intent is created (page load, checkout start),
// never inside the retry loop.
const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

await withRetry(async () => {
  const r = await fetch('/api/orders', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(order),
  });
  if (!r.ok) throw new HttpError(r);
  return r;
});

A new key per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Server: let the database arbitrate

The sketch below uses Express and PostgreSQL. It's an illustration of the pattern: I haven't run the SQL against a live database, so test it in your own stack, including the concurrent case.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key           text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash  text NOT NULL,
  response_code int  NOT NULL,
  response_body jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

// Same payload in a different key order must hash the same.
function canonicalize(v) {
  if (Array.isArray(v)) return v.map(canonicalize);
  if (v && typeof v === 'object') {
    return Object.fromEntries(
      Object.keys(v).sort().map(k => [k, canonicalize(v[k])])
    );
  }
  return v;
}

app.post('/api/orders', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.get('Idempotency-Key');
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key required' });

  const hash = sha256(JSON.stringify(canonicalize(req.body)));
  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    // Claim the key. The PRIMARY KEY decides who wins a race.
    const claim = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash, response_code, response_body)
       VALUES ($1, $2, 0, '{}')
       ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
       RETURNING key`,
      [key, hash]
    );

    if (claim.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      const { rows: [saved] } = await pool.query(
        'SELECT request_hash, response_code, response_body FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = $1',
        [key]
      );
      if (!saved) return res.status(409).set('Retry-After', '1').end(); // first attempt rolled back
      if (saved.request_hash !== hash) {
        return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Key reused with a different payload' });
      }
      return res.status(saved.response_code).json(saved.response_body);
    }

    // We own the key. Do the work, in the same transaction.
    const order = await createOrder(client, req.body);
    const body = { id: order.id };

    await client.query(
      `UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response_code = 201, response_body = $2 WHERE key = $1`,
      [key, body]
    );
    await client.query('COMMIT');
    return res.status(201).json(body);
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK').catch(() => {});
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

Three design points are worth spelling out.

Why INSERT ... ON CONFLICT and not "check, then insert." A SELECT followed by an INSERT has a gap, and two simultaneous requests can both pass the check. Letting a unique constraint decide closes the gap. As I understand PostgreSQL's behavior, a second insert of the same key blocks until the first transaction commits or rolls back, which is why the example doesn't need an in_progress state. Verify that against your isolation level and driver.

Why one transaction. Creating the order and recording the key together means a crash can't leave an order without a key, or a key without an order. This only works when both writes live in the same database. Once the operation involves something outside that transaction (a payment provider, a message queue, an email), the guarantee stops at the transaction boundary. For those, pass a key derived from yours to the provider's own idempotency mechanism, and consider an explicit in_progress state with a defined policy for concurrent callers, such as 409 with Retry-After.

Why canonicalize before hashing. JSON.stringify preserves key order, so {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} hash differently even though they mean the same thing. Without canonicalization, a legitimate retry from a different serializer gets rejected as "key reused with a different payload."

When a simpler rule is enough

If the domain gives you natural uniqueness, such as one open order per (user_id, cart_id), a unique constraint can reject the duplicate without any key table. Idempotency keys are the more general tool, and constraints are the cheaper one when they fit.

Idempotency isn't the only defense either. Uniqueness constraints, transactional design and operation-specific checks all contribute. What an idempotency key gives you that they don't is a consistent answer to the retry: the same response, not an error saying "already exists."

A checklist for the next time you see doubles

  1. Is one of them an OPTIONS preflight?
  2. Does it happen in a production build? If not, check Strict Mode and effect cleanups.
  3. What does the Initiator column say about each request?
  4. How many listeners does the element have?
  5. Does the server log show one request or two? Log a request ID.
  6. Are the two requests identical, or do query strings differ? Different ones suggest a race or dependency-array bug, not a retry.
  7. How far apart are the timestamps? Milliseconds points at a double-click or double-mount. Seconds points at a timeout and retry.
  8. Which layers retry? Browser code, client library, gateway, load balancer, service client, job queue.
  9. Can this endpoint safely run twice? If not, fix that first.

The first eight steps tell you why a duplicate happened. The ninth decides whether it matters.

articles.title: php2shell: a request that fails halfway still leaves state behind
articles.description: Upgrade the PHP runtime itself — to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or your vendor's backported...
articles.body_html:
Upgrade the PHP runtime itself — to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or your vendor's backported package — and restart every worker. Updating WordPress, Drupal, Laravel or a plugin does not fix this one. The two flaws disclosed on 21 October, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 ("php2shell"), live in the runtime, below your application code.

That is why several Government of Canada sites, the STM's site and the SAQ's site went offline on Wednesday as a precaution. Taking a site down until it is patched is a blunt control, but for a bug that can fire before any application code runs, it is a coherent one.

What follows is what I'd want a team to understand before they close the ticket: what failed, what the interim settings do and don't buy you, and the design lesson underneath.

What failed

The PHP security team rates both CVEs critical (CVSS v4.0 9.2). Its advisory describes two related failures:

  • CVE-2026-109618: out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialised, and request cleanup may then treat that data as valid.
  • CVE-2026-109619: request-owned state can survive after its memory has been freed, and a later request handled by the same worker may use it before normal initialisation resets it.

The shared pattern:

  1. A request hits a fatal condition part-way through setup — out-of-memory is the main example — and stops abnormally.
  2. Request-scoped state is left partially initialised, or still referenced after its memory has been freed.
  3. Cleanup, or the next request served by the same worker, trusts that state.

From there, researchers report memory disclosure and remote code execution with the web worker's privileges. Wiz says it demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against WordPress, Drupal and Joomla, and that a trivial "Hello World" script on an affected version can be exposed — the application does not have to do anything wrong.

The PHP team says every installation that serves web requests is at risk: PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. It considers mod_php the highest risk, with a demonstrated exploit that triggers before application code runs.

The design lesson: request isolation is an assumption

PHP's long-standing appeal is the shared-nothing model: each request starts clean and everything is torn down at the end. Long-lived workers make that model an implementation promise rather than a physical fact. The process survives; the runtime is responsible for making each request behave as if it didn't.

php2shell is what it looks like when that promise breaks on the failure path. The happy path resets state. The path where a request dies halfway did not reset it completely, and the next request inherited the residue.

That pattern is not specific to PHP. Anywhere a worker, pool, connection or agent loop is reused, ask the same question: if this unit of work stops at the worst possible line, what does the next unit of work see? Cleanup that only runs on success is not cleanup. It is the same question that sits under retries and partial completion: recovery starts with knowing what state a failed step left behind.

What to do, in order

1. Inventory every PHP runtime, not just your apps. Huntress's list is a good start: web servers, vendor appliances, Windows software that bundles php.exe or php-cgi.exe, control panels such as cPanel and Plesk, container base images, and CMS hosts. php -v on the CLI is not proof of what FPM or mod_php is running; check the SAPI that actually serves traffic.

2. Patch internet-facing systems first, then restart. Fixed upstream releases: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1; those branches no longer receive upstream releases, so check your distribution or LTS vendor. A package upgrade that leaves old FPM workers running has not finished the job.

3. Treat interim settings as partial, because PHP says they are. The advisory lists mitigations while you schedule the upgrade, and states they do not fully protect:

; Interim only — PHP says these do not fully prevent exploitation.
; Restart all workers after changing them.
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0

; Prefer php_admin_value in the FPM pool / Apache config so apps can't override.
post_max_size = 8M        ; 32M if you genuinely accept uploads

; PHP 8.5 only: blocks the confirmed fatal-backtrace path, nothing more.
fatal_error_backtraces = 0

The advisory also suggests memory_limit=-1 paired with a container or cgroup limit that kills only the affected worker, and request limits at the web server or proxy (decoded size, field count, multipart part count, header count, nesting depth). Think about the memory change before applying it: you are trading PHP's own limit for an external one, so the external one has to exist and has to be tight. The advisory specifically warns against using RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation failure.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled in php.ini, the FPM pool or server config. The advisory says not to rely on ini_set() or .user.ini, because the setting has to apply before request parsing.

Hiding errors with display_errors, error_reporting or @ does not help. The issue is the state a fatal error leaves behind, not whether the message is printed.

4. Use a WAF as a layer, not a fix. Cloudflare deployed managed rules about nine hours before disclosure and reports seeing attack traffic and payload mutation against them, and it is explicit that customers still need to patch PHP. By Wednesday evening, watchTowr, Patchstack, Hadrian and others had reported exploitation attempts; watchTowr said none it saw had succeeded yet, and it didn't expect that to last. Edge rules buy time; they do not change the runtime.

5. Look for evidence, since application logs may show little. Because the bug sits below the application, your framework logs may be quiet. Signals the researchers suggest:

  • PHP workers (php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, apache2) spawning sh, bash, python, curl, wget or nc
  • multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors; bursts of HTTP 500s
  • unusually large or malformed PHPSESSID cookies
  • unexplained worker churn
  • new files in the web root, new cron jobs or new accounts

If you find any of these on an unpatched host, isolate it and preserve logs before you rebuild.

The patch window is shorter now

Two details from the timeline matter for planning. First, Calif reports finding the first issue on 1 August using GPT-5.6 Sol, and Wiz found it independently on 19 August with its own tooling and frontier models; OpenAI and the PHP team both warn that the same capabilities help attackers build exploits. Second, a leak on 20 October pulled the coordinated release forward by a day.

I don't think the useful conclusion is alarm. It is operational: the time between "fix available" and "exploit attempts observed" was, by Cloudflare's account, close to zero this week. Teams that can answer where does PHP run, who owns it, and how fast can we restart it in an hour are in a different position from teams that discover the answer during the incident.

Exposure is also not the same as market share. The widely quoted "70 per cent" figure is PHP's share of websites, not a count of exploitable hosts; Palo Alto Networks' initial estimate, as reported by Fortune, was 22.6 million potentially vulnerable instances. Exploit reliability varies with version, configuration and memory layout. Patch anyway — but plan from your own inventory, not the headline.

Sources

  • Official advisory, fixed versions and mitigations: PHP security advisory, 21 Oct 2026, GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618), GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619)
  • Timeline and detection guidance: Huntress
  • Fixed versions, affected SAPIs and partial mitigations: BleepingComputer
  • Root cause, discovery timeline and indicators: Wiz
  • Edge protections and observed attack traffic: Cloudflare
  • Exploitation attempts: SecurityWeek
  • Discovery dates, exposure estimate and quotes: Fortune
  • Canadian takedowns: CP24

Facts checked against the PHP advisory and the sources above on the evening of 21 October 2026. I'll update this post if the guidance changes.

articles.title: AI Made Everything Look the Same. That’s the Frontend’s Best News in a Decade.
articles.description: You can spot it in two seconds   Open any landing page launched in the last year and give...
articles.body_html:
You can spot it in two seconds

Open any landing page launched in the last year and give yourself two seconds. You already know whether a person made it.

The gradient hero. The three feature cards in a row, each with a tiny icon in a tinted circle. Everything rounded exactly the same amount. A "Get started" button, a "See how it works" button next to it in ghost style. Inter, or whatever Inter is wearing this month. A purple that fades into a blue. Scroll and there's a logo wall of companies that have never heard of the product.

None of this is wrong. That's the uncomfortable part. Every one of those choices is defensible on its own. Together they produce a page that could belong to any of ten thousand companies, and your brain files it under "nobody was here" before you've read a word.

People started calling this AI slop somewhere around 2024 and it stuck, because it names a feeling we all had and couldn't explain. Same thing happened with AI images a year earlier. The hands got fixed. The skin got fixed. And still, you can tell.

Everyone got the order wrong

When the image models landed, the joke was that designers were first in line. Then Copilot and Cursor and the rest showed up and the joke moved to frontend. Backend was supposed to be safe. Distributed systems, consistency guarantees, all that hard stuff. The real engineering.

I've spent twelve years on the frontend side of that line and I think it's backwards.

Here is the claim, and the rest of this post is me trying to earn it: the more AI makes everything look the same, the more the interface becomes the only part of a product that can still be different. Backend converging on sameness is a feature. Frontend converging on sameness is a funeral.

Backend is the easier target, and nobody minds

Think about what makes a task easy for a model. It wants a well-documented problem, a known good shape for the answer, and a way to check whether it got it right.

Backend has all three.

The patterns are written down. Not just written down, written down by the people who scaled them. Every big tech engineering blog is a free textbook on queues, caches, sharding, idempotency, retries. The reasoning behind each decision is public. There's a word for the ideal backend and it is "boring". Boring is a compliment. Nobody opens a status page and thinks "I wish this Postgres felt more personal".

Correctness is checkable. Tests pass or they don't. p99 is under the budget or it isn't. The contract is the OpenAPI spec and the model can read it.

And the user never sees it. This is the big one. If your API is shaped like Stripe's and your queue is shaped like everyone's queue, your customer will never know and would not care if they did. Sameness costs you nothing here. It is literally best practice.

Someone will say "try vibe-coding a consensus protocol". Fair. The hard five percent of backend stays hard. It also lives in maybe fifty companies on earth. The median backend is a CRUD app with a job runner and a cache, and that shape has been solved so many times the model has seen it from every angle.

What I saw when I built the pipeline myself

I'm not arguing from the sidelines. I built a Figma-to-code pipeline on top of MCP. Designer finishes a frame, the pipeline reads it, maps it onto our existing component library, and hands back a working React screen that uses our buttons and our inputs and our spacing tokens instead of inventing new ones.

It worked. Better than I expected. Settings pages, forms, tables, modals, the whole middle of the app came out usable on the first pass most of the time. The kind of screen a mid-level engineer would have spent a day and a half on became a twenty-minute review.

Here's what it never did well, and I watched it try for months.

It could not decide what was worth being different. Hand it a frame where the designer had done something slightly odd on purpose, a card that breaks the grid, a transition that lingers a beat longer than it should, and it would quietly regularise it. Snap the card back to the grid. Use the default easing. Not because it was wrong, because the odd thing didn't match anything in the library and the safest move was to pick the nearest known shape.

That is the exact behaviour that produces slop. Not errors. Safety. A thousand locally reasonable choices that add up to a page with no fingerprints on it.

The human in the loop wasn't there to fix bugs. The human was there to say "no, leave that weird, it's the point".

Taste has no spec

Now run the backend checklist against the frontend.

Well-documented problem? Sort of. There are design systems and WCAG and a hundred "best practices" posts. But none of them tell you what your product should feel like. There is no engineering blog that explains why Linear feels like Linear.

Known good shape? That's the trap. There is a known good shape. It's the one from the first section. Following it is how you end up looking like everyone.

A way to check? A user looks at the screen for two hundred milliseconds and decides whether they trust you. There's no test for that. There's no p99 for "this looks like somebody cared".

And this is the part that holds up even as the models get better. Being distinctive is relative. The moment a style is learnable and common, it stops being distinctive by definition. Whatever the model converges on becomes the new default, and the new default is exactly what people learn to see through. The target moves every time it's hit. A model that nails today's taste is producing tomorrow's tell.

Meanwhile features have become table stakes. Anyone can clone your feature list over a weekend now. Nobody is choosing you for having a dashboard. What's left to choose on is how it feels to use the thing, and that is the surface.

Imperfect is not the same as bad

I keep hearing "people want human imperfection in UI now" and I want to be careful with it, because it's half right and the wrong half is dangerous.

Nobody wants a misaligned button. Nobody misses the 2009 web.

What people respond to is intention. A choice that a template would never make, made on purpose, and then committed to. Linear's keyboard-first everything. Arc's sidebar that refused to look like a browser. Raycast's little animations that nobody asked for. These are not imperfect products. They're extremely polished. They're just polished in a direction nobody else picked.

The tell for slop isn't ugliness. It's the absence of a decision. You look at a page and can't find a single spot where someone chose the harder option because they liked it better.

So if you're a frontend person reading this and feeling relieved, don't get the wrong idea. The job isn't to add quirks. The job is to have opinions and ship them. That was always the job. It's just that for a while, shipping fast could cover for not having any. It can't anymore, because fast is free now.

"The future has no UI"

There's a camp that says all of this is moot because the interface is going away. You'll talk to an agent, it'll call the APIs, work gets done, no screens. Who needs a frontend when you can just ask.

I'd buy it if I knew what I wanted every time I opened an app. I don't. Most people don't.

Think about how you actually use the big consumer products. You open Spotify without a song in mind. You open YouTube without a query. You open a shopping site to see what's there. You scroll Instagram to be shown things. Half the money in consumer software comes from people who arrived with no intent and left having found something. That's discovery, and discovery is a browsing problem.

Agents are great at retrieval. "Book me the 7am flight." "Find the invoice from March." Clear ask, clear answer, no screen needed, fine. But a chat box is a terrible place to not know what you want. A blank input with a blinking cursor is the least helpful interface ever designed for someone who hasn't decided yet. A good grid of options beats it every time.

So yes, a chunk of the interface will disappear, the chunk that was only ever a form in front of an API. That chunk was already the boring part. What's left is the part where someone has to be shown something they didn't ask for and be glad about it. That part gets more important, not less.

Where the value goes

When building something is free, the value moves to whatever isn't. I count three things: distribution, trust, and the way the product feels in your hands. Two of those three live in the interface. A page that looks generated now reads as "we didn't care enough to be here", and that's a trust problem before it's a design problem.

I'll put a prediction down so you have something to argue with. Within two years, "must not look AI-generated" shows up as a line item in design briefs, written down, the way "must be mobile responsive" did ten years ago. And somewhere right now, someone is building a product whose entire edge is that it looks like a person made it. I'd bet on them.

Backend engineers, you're fine. Boring was always the goal, and you're about to get very good at it very cheaply.

Frontend people, the bar just moved. Not down. Up, and sideways, to a place the models can't follow because the moment they get there it stops being the place.

articles.title: AI Made Coding Cheaper. So Why Is Building Software Still So Expensive?
articles.description: I can generate a full authentication flow with a database schema, API routes, and unit tests in under...
articles.body_html:
I can generate a full authentication flow with a database schema, API routes, and unit tests in under 30 seconds.

I can refactor a messy component into clean React hooks with one prompt.

I can ask an AI to explain a complex regex, and it will break it down for me line by line.

So why did my last "simple" feature still take three weeks to reach production?

If writing code is now practically free, why does building software still feel so incredibly expensive?

The Paradox of the 30-Second Pull Request

Last month, I was working on a feature that usually takes a few days. I fired up Cursor (or your AI tool of choice), typed a detailed prompt, and watched the code materialize on my screen.

It was beautiful. Clean. Formatted.

I felt like a 10x developer. I opened a Pull Request that same afternoon, feeling incredibly proud of my "velocity."

Then the real work started.

It took my teammate two days to review it. Not because the code was wrong, but because the AI had introduced a subtle edge case in the caching logic that neither of us initially understood.

When we finally deployed it, it broke a legacy system that the AI didn't even know existed.

We spent the next week debugging, rolling back, and rewriting the "perfect" AI-generated code to fit our actual, messy production environment.

That's when the uncomfortable realization hit me:

Writing the code was never the expensive part. It was always the cheapest part.

The Jevons Paradox in Software Engineering

In economics, there's a concept called the Jevons Paradox. It states that as technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, total consumption of that resource may actually increase, rather than decrease.

AI made writing code cheap. So what happened? We just demanded more code.

When it took a week to write a feature, we shipped one feature. Now that it takes an hour to write the code, management asks for five features in the same week.

But the bottleneck of software engineering was never typing speed. It's not the syntax. It's the cognitive load of context.

AI doesn't know your company's three-year-old architectural decisions. It doesn't know why that one microservice is fragile. It doesn't know the business logic that lives in the head of the developer who left the company two years ago.

So where did the cost go? It shifted to three places we rarely measure:

1. The Review and Trust Tax

Reading code is vastly harder than writing it. When a human writes code, you can ask them, "Why did you do it this way?" When AI writes code, you have to reverse-engineer its logic just to trust it. We are now spending more time reviewing code than we ever did writing it.

2. The Context Debt

AI is a brilliant sprinter, but a terrible architect. It can build a function perfectly, but it doesn't understand how that function breaks the other 50,000 lines of code in your repository. The "integration cost" of AI code is astronomically high.

3. The Maintenance Bill

Generating code is cheap. Maintaining generative code is expensive. AI often writes code that is technically correct but idiomatically weird. It creates abstractions that don't make sense to humans. And six months from now, someone is going to have to read it.

How We Actually Fix This

If code is cheap, we have to stop optimizing for typing speed. We have to start optimizing for decision-making.

1. Move the bottleneck to design.
Don't prompt AI to "build this feature." Prompt it to "suggest three architectural approaches." Spend the saved time deciding which approach is best for your specific context.

2. Protect your review capacity.
Your senior developers are now bottlenecks. If an AI generates 1,000 lines of code, the senior developer's brain is the only thing standing between that code and production. Buy them more time for review.

3. Focus on "Delete" over "Write".
The best use of AI is not to add new code, but to delete old code. Use it to untangle messes, write missing tests, and refactor legacy systems. Use the speed to reduce your maintenance burden.

The uncomfortable truth

AI didn't make software engineering easier.

It just changed the job from "writing code" to "editing code."

And editing requires a deeper understanding of the system than writing ever did.

If you don't understand the code an AI generated for you, you don't own that code. The code owns you. And the debt you are accumulating is going to come due.

Writing code is now a commodity. Understanding what to build, how it fits into the big picture, and how to keep it secure is where the real value lies.

You don't need to be a faster coder anymore. You need to be a better systems thinker.

Now I'm curious, because I know I'm not the only one feeling this shift.

Have you noticed that AI has made you type faster, but your features still take just as long to ship? Where is the biggest bottleneck on your team right now?

Is it the reviews? The testing? The architecture?

Drop it in the comments below. Let's figure out what the new "10x developer" actually looks like.

articles.title: Don't Be a Proxy Between Me and Your AI
articles.description: I've had this conversation more times than I'd like to admit.  I raise a technical question in a...
articles.body_html:
I've had this conversation more times than I'd like to admit.

I raise a technical question in a thread, a meeting, or a design review and someone responds with a long, well-structured, suspiciously balanced answer. It has headers in spirit if not in format, it covers 3 tradeoffs and ends with a neat recommendation.

I push back on one point. Silence for a minute, the kind where you can practically hear a browser tab switching. Then another equally polished paragraph appears, answering my pushback.

At some point it kinda gives: I'm not talking to a colleague. I'm talking to a chat window with a human-shaped copy-paste button attached.

please stop doing that, I'm practically begging you.

I Can Open a Browser Too

Let me say the obvious thing first. If I wanted to debate an AI, I'd debate an AI. I can type a question into ChatGPT, Claude, or whatever else is in vogue this week. It takes me 10 seconds, and I'd get to skip the middleman. Right now you're less a colleague and more a loading spinner with a LinkedIn profile.

When I bring a technical question to you, I’m asking for your judgment. What you’ve seen work, what you’ve watched fail, and what taught you the difference. I want to know which tradeoffs you’d accept, which assumptions you’d challenge, and why. That’s the experience I’m interested in hearing.

The moment you become a pass-through, I lose all of that. I'm getting generic output with your name on it, and you've added latency to the conversation without adding anything else. Congratulations, you've invented the world's slowest API wrapper.

"But I'm the Decision-Maker"

This is the one that really gets me.

The pitch goes like this: in the AI era, the developer's job is to be the "architect". The AI generates the options, the human decides. You're like the guardrail, the one with taste.

Fine model. I think it's genuinely where a lot of the job is heading.

But a decision-maker who agrees with the AI's recommendation 99% of the time isn't deciding anything. That's a rubber stamp with a job title. If your "decisions" are indistinguishable from the model's default output, then you haven't added a layer of judgment, you've just added a layer of delay.

So here's a simple test: can you name a recent time you disagreed with the AI, and why? Not "I tweaked the formatting." A real disagreement, grounded in something the model couldn't know, like a constraint, a past incident, or a team preference.

If you can't, you're not the guardrail. You're the passenger and you didn't even pick the playlist.

I have a good, real example of this:

Someone messaged me on LinkedIn, saying they were interested in learning how I approach problems in distributed systems. I'll be honest: that's the kind of message that makes my day. A person wants to talk shop, and wants my thinking.

So I engaged. I walked through how I reason about failure modes and where I start when things go inconsistent and we went back and forth for a while.

Then I found out they'd been using an AI to debate me the whole time. They hadn't come to learn from me at all. They'd come to argue with me through a proxy.

And here's the thing: I debate AI every day. By choice, on my own terms, whenever I feel like it. That part is easy to get. What's rare is another human being who's actually willing to sit in the conversation, think out loud, be wrong in front of me, and push back with their own head.

If they'd just asked me their own half-formed questions, I'd have answered them all day.

"Whatever the AI Said Is What I Agree With"

This is the response I get when I ask the follow-up: "What's the point of discussing this if your brain isn't the one engaging?"

"Oh, well, it's what I agree with anyway."

Bold of you to agree so passionately with a position you didn't form.

Agreement without understanding is not the same as agreement. If I ask why you agree and the honest answer is "because it said so and it sounded right," then you don't hold a position but a borrowed one.

And borrowed positions collapse under the first real question, like a Jenga tower in a minor earthquake. I wrote about this before: reading something and nodding is not the same skill as being able to produce or defend it. A discussion is exactly the situation that exposes the gap, which is why it matters.

And about the "I'm verifying the output" defense: verification is real work. It means checking claims against reality, testing assumptions, and spotting what's subtly wrong. If your verification consists of reading the answer and thinking "yep, sounds right," that's not a guardrail, that's reading. A guardrail that never catches anything is just a decorative pool noodle.

"I Don't Have Time, I'm Busy"

classic. "I just don't have time to dig into this, so I asked the AI."

Yah yah, you're busy but so is everyone. I am busy. The person you're talking to is busy. The barista making your oat flat white is busy. Busy is not a personality. Being busy isn't a special condition you hold exclusively and it doesn't excuse you from engaging with the thing you chose to join a discussion about.

But notice the quiet logic buried in that excuse: if you don't have time to engage, you also don't have time to be in the conversation. There's a clean, honorable option here, and it's just saying so:

"I don't have the bandwidth to think this through properly. I'd rather not give you a half-answer. Can we circle back later today?"

It's respectable, It's honest, it respects my time and it doesn't pretend. What's not respectable is dumping unvetted output into the thread and presenting it as your contribution.

The Fair Counterargument

Before this turns into pure ranting, let me steelman the other side and because there are legitimate reasons someone leans on AI in discussions:

  • Language. If English isn’t your first language, using AI to polish your phrasing is a perfectly good use. What matters is that the ideas are yours. And honestly, I don’t care if your spelling or grammar is rough. I’m a software engineer, not an English literature professor. The point of language is to communicate ideas. If I understand what you’re trying to say—and 99% of the time, I do—we’re good.
  • Preparation. Using AI to explore a topic beforehand, surface counterarguments, or sanity-check your thinking is great. That's research.
  • Juniors learning. Someone new may reach for AI because they don't yet have the experience to form an opinion. That's understandable, and the fix is mentoring, not shaming.

I don't have a problem with AI being in the process. I have a problem with AI replacing the person in the process.

The line, I think, is this: did you take the model's output and make it yours? Did you push on it, disagree with parts of it, and rewrite it in terms of your actual situation? Or did you relay it?

Try these

Here's how I think AI belongs in a technical discussion:

  1. Use it before the conversation, not during it. Ask it to stress-test your idea. Ask it for the strongest objection. Then think about the answer.
  2. Form a position you can defend without it. If someone challenges you and you'd need to go back to the chat window to answer, you're not ready to answer.
  3. Be upfront about what's yours and what isn't. "I asked an AI for options and I'm leaning toward B because of X" is excellent. The "because of X" is the part that proves a human was involved.
  4. Disagree with it sometimes, on purpose. If you never override the model, ask yourself whether you're evaluating it or just following it.
  5. When you don't know, say so. "I don't know, let me find out" has never made anyone look incompetent. Faking it with someone else's words eventually does.

Why This Matters Beyond Politeness

It's tempting to file all of this under "annoying etiquette," but I think it's bigger than that.

Technical discussion is how teams build a shared mental model. It's where assumptions get surfaced, where one person's experience corrects another's blind spot, and where the real reasoning behind decisions gets created and recorded. If one side of the conversation is hollow, the team walks away with a decision that nobody actually reasoned about.

That's the same cognitive-debt problem I keep writing about, just moved from code into conversation. And like all debt, it comes due at a bad moment, usually when the decision turns out to be wrong and someone asks, "Why did we choose this?" and the honest answer is "the AI said so, and we all kind of nodded."

Conclusion

Use AI. Use it constantly, if it makes you better. But when you sit down to talk to another human about a hard problem, show up.

Bring your own opinions, even imperfect ones, bring your own doubts, bring the thing you know that the model doesn't. That's the only thing I came to the conversation for.

Because if I wanted the average of the internet's opinion, I'd have asked the internet. Human engagement is the rare thing now so please don't be the reason it gets rarer.

articles.title: Where Do Your Users' Passwords Actually Live? Self-Hosted vs Managed Keycloak
articles.description: Choosing between self-hosted and managed Keycloak affects more than where your identity service runs....
articles.body_html:
Choosing between self-hosted and managed Keycloak affects more than where your identity service runs. It determines who maintains the infrastructure, who handles security updates, and how much responsibility your team takes on when users need to authenticate.

When you add authentication to an application, it's easy to focus on the login screen. You choose between passwords and passkeys, connect an identity provider, and make sure users can access their accounts. But there's another question worth asking before your application goes live: where are your users' credentials stored, and who is responsible for protecting them?

Keycloak gives developers control over authentication and identity management. You can run it on infrastructure you manage, or use a managed Keycloak service that takes care of much of the underlying operation.

Both approaches can work well. The right choice depends on your security requirements, your team's infrastructure experience, your budget, and how much operational responsibility you're prepared to take on.

Let's look at what happens to user passwords in each setup, what changes when you choose a managed service, and how to decide which option makes sense for your application.

TL;DR

With self-hosted Keycloak, user credentials are stored in the Keycloak database that you configure and operate. Your team is responsible for securing that database, maintaining backups, applying updates, and protecting the infrastructure.

With Skycloak's managed Keycloak, you use the official upstream Keycloak platform without operating the underlying identity infrastructure yourself. Skycloak manages the infrastructure and provides automatic updates, while your team retains control over Keycloak configuration and remains responsible for integrating authentication securely into your application.

Here's the practical difference:

  • Self-hosted Keycloak: You control the deployment, database, network, updates, backups, and access policies. You also carry the operational burden of keeping everything secure and available.
  • Managed Keycloak with Skycloak: Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure while giving your team full Keycloak admin access. All plans support unlimited users, so pricing isn't tied to monthly active users.
  • Regions and portability: Skycloak offers deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia, plus realm export options to help you plan a migration if you later choose to self-host.
  • Getting started: You can try Skycloak free for 21 days without providing a credit card.
  • Password security: Keycloak stores passwords as salted password hashes, not as readable plaintext passwords. Database access, configuration, backups, and administrative permissions still need protection.
  • Cost: Self-hosting can offer more infrastructure control, but server costs are only part of the total expense. Managed services add a service fee but can reduce the engineering time spent operating the identity platform.

The short answer: In a standard deployment, Keycloak handles authentication in both models. The main difference is who operates the identity infrastructure and how responsibilities are divided between your team and the provider. If you use an external user store, credential storage and verification may be handled partly or entirely by that system.

What Actually Happens to a Password in Keycloak?

Imagine someone creates an account in your application. They enter an email address, choose a password, and click Create account. Where does that password go?

In a typical Keycloak setup using its built-in user storage, Keycloak receives the password during account creation and stores a password hash in its configured database. A password hash is the output of a one-way password-hashing function. When the user signs in later, Keycloak verifies the submitted password against the stored hash. If an external user store handles authentication, credential storage and verification may follow a different process.

The database doesn't need to contain the original password in readable form. Keycloak uses a password-hashing algorithm and configuration designed to make guessing passwords computationally expensive. The exact algorithm and parameters depend on the Keycloak version and configuration.

Keycloak's default password-hashing algorithm depends on the version and deployment configuration. Keycloak 24 changed the default from pbkdf2-sha256 to pbkdf2-sha512. Starting with Keycloak 25, Argon2 became the default for non-FIPS deployments, while FIPS deployments use a compatible algorithm such as pbkdf2-sha512. Existing credentials may retain their previous hash until the user next signs in and Keycloak re-hashes the password under the current configuration.

To inspect or configure password policy settings, open the Keycloak Admin Console and navigate to Authentication → Policies → Password policy.

Review the policy configured for your realm before assuming it matches the defaults for a particular release.

Where Keycloak Stores Password Credentials

In a standard Keycloak deployment using its built-in user storage, password credentials are stored in the database configured for Keycloak. The CREDENTIAL table holds credential records associated with users, including password-related data and metadata.

Two fields help illustrate how that works:

  • SECRET_DATA: stores sensitive credential data, including password-hashing information.
  • CREDENTIAL_DATA: stores additional credential metadata, such as information about the credential type and its configuration.

These fields contain structured data, not a readable copy of the user's original password. The exact contents depend on the credential type and Keycloak version.

For example, a password credential record may contain data resembling the following. These are illustrative examples, not actual values from a live Keycloak database.

// SECRET_DATA — illustrative example
{
  "value": "[password hash omitted]",
  "salt": "[salt omitted]",
  "additionalParameters": {}
}

// CREDENTIAL_DATA — illustrative example
{
  "algorithm": "argon2",
  "hashIterations": "[configured value]",
  "additionalParameters": {}
}

The exact field names and structure can vary by Keycloak version and credential implementation.

Password Hashing Isn't the Whole Security Story

This distinction matters because password hashing and database security solve different problems. Hashing helps protect passwords if someone obtains a copy of the credential records, but it doesn't make a compromised identity server or database harmless. Attackers who gain administrative access may be able to alter accounts, change authentication settings, or access other sensitive information.

For example, your deployment still needs to protect:

  • Database access and administrative credentials.
  • Backups containing credential records and other sensitive data.
  • Keycloak configuration and privileged administrative accounts.
  • The infrastructure and network surrounding the identity service.

Where Is the Rest of the Identity Data Stored?

Your Keycloak deployment also holds information beyond password credentials, including user profiles, groups, roles, and configuration data. Depending on your setup, it may connect to external identity providers or use additional user-storage systems. The exact location of user data therefore depends on how the realm and user storage are configured.

For a standard deployment using Keycloak's built-in user storage, the password hashes are held in the configured database. If your environment uses an external user store, the credentials may be managed there instead.

This is the starting point for comparing self-hosted and managed Keycloak: the credential-handling model can remain the same, while the people responsible for the surrounding infrastructure change.

What Self-Hosted Keycloak Means

With self-hosted Keycloak, you deploy and operate the identity service on infrastructure under your team's control. That might be a virtual machine, a container platform, Kubernetes, or another supported environment.

You choose the deployment architecture, configure the database, manage network access, and decide how the service fits into your existing infrastructure. This gives you considerable flexibility, which can be valuable when an application has specific compliance requirements or needs to integrate with internal systems.

What Your Team Is Responsible For

The trade-off is that your team must take responsibility for operating the service reliably.

That includes:

  • Applying Keycloak security updates and testing upgrades.
  • Maintaining the database and testing backups and restores.
  • Monitoring availability and planning for service failures.
  • Protecting administrative accounts, TLS certificates, and network rules.
  • Reviewing configuration changes and tracking security advisories.

There's also the less visible work: testing recovery procedures and making sure they still work when you need them.

When Does Self-Hosting Make Sense?

Self-hosting can be a good fit when you need deep infrastructure control and have the people and processes to maintain it. It can also make sense when your organization already operates identity infrastructure and has established procedures for security, monitoring, and incident response.

But running Keycloak yourself doesn't automatically make your authentication more secure. The result depends on how well the service, database, network, and operational processes are configured and maintained.

What Changes With Managed Keycloak?

Managed Keycloak shifts much of the infrastructure work to a service provider. You still use Keycloak for identity management and authentication, but the provider operates the managed environment according to its service offering.

For a development team, that can mean less time spent maintaining servers, planning upgrades, monitoring infrastructure, and managing database operations. It can also make it easier to get an identity service running without first building an entire deployment and maintenance process.

What the Provider May Manage

The provider may manage:

  • Infrastructure provisioning and maintenance.
  • Database operations and backups.
  • Keycloak updates and upgrades.
  • Availability monitoring and infrastructure recovery.

What Still Belongs to Your Team?

However, managed Keycloak doesn't mean someone else automatically handles every aspect of authentication security.

Your team still needs to configure authentication flows, manage realm settings, assign appropriate roles, protect administrative access, and integrate the identity provider correctly with your application. You also need to decide how users are onboarded, how accounts are recovered, and what permissions they receive after signing in.

Data ownership and access deserve attention, too. Before choosing a provider, understand where your identity data is stored, who can access it, how backups are protected, and what happens when you decide to leave the service.

Managed Keycloak is useful when you want to use Keycloak's identity capabilities without taking on the full burden of operating the infrastructure.

Self-Hosted Keycloak vs Skycloak: A Practical Comparison

Both deployment models can use Keycloak's authentication features. The differences become clearer when you compare the responsibilities involved in running them.

Area Self-hosted Keycloak Skycloak
Infrastructure Your team provisions and operates it Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure
Database operations Your team configures, secures, and maintains the database Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure
Security updates Your team plans, tests, and applies updates Automatic updates
Backups and recovery Your team configures and tests backup and restore procedures Skycloak manages infrastructure, updates, backups, and scaling
Availability Your team designs and maintains availability Uptime commitments vary by plan; Business includes a 99.9% SLA, and Enterprise offers up to 99.99%
Configuration control Greater control over the deployment environment Full Keycloak admin access; Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure
Operational workload Higher infrastructure responsibility Reduced infrastructure maintenance for your team
Cost structure Infrastructure, engineering time, maintenance, and operational overhead Infrastructure-based pricing, unlimited users, and no fees tied to monthly active users

Self-hosted Keycloak gives your team direct control over the infrastructure and responsibility for operating it. Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure, while your team retains full Keycloak admin access and responsibility for securely integrating authentication into your application. All Skycloak plans support unlimited users, with pricing based on infrastructure rather than monthly active users.

Cost also deserves a realistic comparison. A self-hosted deployment might look cheaper when you compare only server expenses with a managed service's monthly fee. Once you include engineering time, monitoring, backups, upgrades, incident response, and availability requirements, the total cost can look different.

For a small team, reducing ongoing operational work may justify a managed service. For an organization with a mature platform engineering team and strict infrastructure requirements, self-hosting may be the better fit.

How Skycloak Makes Managed Keycloak Practical

Self-hosting Keycloak gives your team control, but that control comes with ongoing work: maintaining the deployment, applying updates, monitoring availability, and keeping the supporting infrastructure secure.

Skycloak provides managed hosting for upstream Keycloak. It manages the underlying infrastructure while giving your team full Keycloak admin access, so you can configure identity and authentication without operating the infrastructure yourself.

Keep Keycloak's Capabilities Without Running the Infrastructure

Skycloak runs upstream Keycloak and gives your team full Keycloak admin access. Its managed service includes the following benefits:

  • Less infrastructure maintenance: Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure, reducing the operational work your team handles.
  • Keycloak authentication features: Configure SSO, MFA, SAML, and OpenID Connect (OIDC).
  • Unlimited users: All plans support unlimited users, with no fees tied to monthly active users.
  • Regional deployment options: Paid plans offer supported deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia.
  • Realm export: Export your realms to help plan a migration to a self-hosted Keycloak deployment.
  • Free trial: Try Skycloak for 21 days without a credit card.

For current pricing and plan details, visit the Skycloak pricing page.

What Does This Mean for Your Team?

Consider a small SaaS team building its product. The developers need authentication, user management, and secure access to application resources, but they may not have a dedicated platform team to maintain an identity deployment.

With self-hosted Keycloak, the team plans and maintains infrastructure provisioning, updates, backups, monitoring, and recovery alongside product development. With Skycloak, the provider manages the underlying infrastructure, while the team focuses on integrating Keycloak, configuring authentication flows, managing access, and securing application sessions.

This doesn't remove the need for sound identity and application security. Your team still needs to configure roles and permissions, protect administrative access, validate redirect URIs, and make sure authenticated users can access only the resources they're authorized to use.

The benefit is a clearer division of responsibilities: Skycloak operates the managed infrastructure, while your team focuses on using Keycloak securely within the application.

Is Skycloak Worth Considering?

Skycloak is worth considering if you want Keycloak's flexibility without operating the underlying infrastructure. All plans support unlimited users, and infrastructure-based pricing means your bill isn't tied to monthly active users. You can choose from supported deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia, export realms when planning a migration, and try the service free for 21 days without a credit card.

Compare the available features and prices on the Skycloak pricing page.

Which Keycloak Deployment Should You Choose?

There's no universal winner. The right choice depends on your team's capabilities and the requirements of your application.

Choose self-hosted Keycloak if:

  • You need extensive control over the infrastructure, network, database, or deployment architecture.
  • Your organization already has people responsible for operating production services.
  • You have specific requirements that a managed provider cannot meet.
  • You're prepared to maintain upgrades, backups, monitoring, incident response, and disaster recovery.

Choose managed Keycloak with Skycloak if:

  • You want upstream Keycloak without operating the underlying identity infrastructure.
  • You want full Keycloak admin access while reducing infrastructure maintenance.
  • You need features such as SSO, MFA, OIDC, and SAML.
  • You want unlimited users without fees tied to monthly active users.
  • You need deployment options in the US, EU, Canada, or Australia.
  • Realm export and a 21-day free trial without a credit card fit your evaluation and migration plans.

For an early-stage SaaS product, Skycloak can provide a way to use Keycloak without building and maintaining the supporting infrastructure from scratch. Teams with established platform engineering capabilities or requirements that call for direct infrastructure control may prefer self-hosting. Evaluate both options against your security needs, engineering capacity, expected costs, and long-term plans.

Before committing, ask a few concrete questions: Can you configure the authentication flows you need? Can you export or migrate your identity data? What backup and recovery guarantees exist? Who applies security updates, and how are changes communicated? What happens if the provider experiences an outage?

Those answers will tell you more than the label managed or self-hosted alone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where does Keycloak store user passwords?

→ In a standard Keycloak deployment using its built-in user storage, password credentials are stored as password hashes in the configured database. Keycloak does not need to store the original passwords in readable plaintext. If the deployment uses an external user store, credential storage may be handled by that system.

What is Skycloak, and how does it differ from self-hosted Keycloak?

→ Skycloak is a managed Keycloak service that runs the upstream Keycloak platform and manages the underlying infrastructure. With self-hosted Keycloak, your team operates the deployment and supporting services. With Skycloak, infrastructure responsibilities covered by the service move to the provider, while your team continues to manage application integration and identity configuration.

Can I use passkeys with self-hosted and managed Keycloak?

→ Yes. Keycloak supports WebAuthn-based authentication, including passwordless passkey flows, when configured appropriately. The exact setup depends on your Keycloak version, authentication flow, and environment. With a managed service, confirm that the provider supports the configuration and administrative access your application needs.

Who manages security when using Skycloak?

→ Security responsibilities are shared. Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure, while your team uses its full Keycloak admin access to configure authentication, protect administrative accounts, assign appropriate permissions, and integrate Keycloak securely into the application. Your team should still verify any specific uptime, backup, and recovery commitments it requires.

Is self-hosted Keycloak cheaper than managed Keycloak?

→ It can be, but server costs alone don't show the full picture. Self-hosting also requires engineering time for updates, monitoring, backups, troubleshooting, and incident response. Managed Keycloak introduces service fees but may reduce those operational costs. Compare the total cost of ownership for your expected workload and team capacity.

Final Thoughts

Self-hosting gives you direct responsibility for the deployment, database, updates, and availability. Skycloak lets you keep using upstream Keycloak with full Keycloak admin access while the provider manages the underlying infrastructure.

All plans support unlimited users, and the service offers deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia. You can try Skycloak for free for 21 days without a credit card.

Choose the setup that protects your users' identities and gives your team a clear, sustainable way to manage authentication as your product grows.
