  • Entire — the agent session above shows how it was built, the jsDelivr dependency that had to be removed, and the failure I chose to document instead of hide.

articles.title: We let Oxlint loose on a real React codebase. The speed wasn't the surprise.
articles.description: In 1787, Thomas Rowlandson drew an ox loose on Westminster Bridge. Hats flying, people climbing the...
articles.body_html:
In 1787, Thomas Rowlandson drew an ox loose on Westminster Bridge. Hats flying, people climbing the railings, total panic.

That's roughly how it feels to drop a Rust linter into a five-year-old JavaScript project.

Oxlint and Oxfmt are the linter and formatter from the Oxc project. Between them they're downloaded about 26 million times a week, and the docs make bold claims: Oxlint is "50 to 100 times faster than ESLint", and Oxfmt is "approximately 30x faster than Prettier."

Bold claims deserve a stopwatch. So we picked a real, popular React codebase and timed both setups on the same laptop.

But the stopwatch turned out to be the boring part.

The test

We used Excalidraw, the open-source whiteboard app. It's a big React + TypeScript codebase (710 JS/TS files) with the setup a lot of teams still have: ESLint 7 using Create React App's rules, with Prettier 2.6 running inside ESLint as a plugin.

The machine was an ordinary laptop: Ryzen 5 5600H, 12 threads, 15 GB RAM. Each command got one warm-up run and three timed runs, and we report the median (the middle one).

What we ran Time
ESLint + Prettier plugin (how Excalidraw ships it) 60.2 s
ESLint with the Prettier rule switched off 50.7 s
Prettier 2.6 --check on its own 15.3 s
Oxlint, with Excalidraw's rules ported over 1.5 s
Oxfmt --check 0.41 s

So the full check went from one minute to about two seconds. That's roughly 30x faster: real, but well short of the "50 to 100x" headline. The gap makes sense, because every plugin you switch on costs time. Oxlint with zero config took 0.46 s; with React, import and accessibility rules on, it took 1.3–1.5 s.

One bonus finding before we move on: the Prettier plugin alone cost about 10 seconds per run. If you run Prettier inside ESLint, you can split them apart today without switching any tools.

The part nobody puts in the benchmark

ESLint reported 0 warnings. Oxlint, with the same rules ported over, reported 435 warnings and 1 error.

At first glance that looks like Oxlint found 435 bugs that ESLint missed. It didn't. When we went through them:

  • 145 were unused variables and parameters. Oxlint's version of the rule is stricter by default.
  • 48 of the 50 "this number loses precision" warnings came from one file: a table of 40-digit math constants, written that way on purpose.
  • The 1 error was a target="_blank" link that already had rel="noopener", built from a template string. Excalidraw had already told ESLint to skip that check on that line.

Then the useful ones. Oxlint's React rules flagged 22 places that call setState directly inside an effect (the newer React guidance says to calculate the value during render instead) and 10 async Promise executors. Those are worth a look. ESLint 7's old rules simply don't know about them.

So here's the honest version:

  • First 2 seconds: "wow."
  • Next 20 minutes: "wait, which of these are real?"
  • Next week: "who decides which rules we actually want?"

The speed is free. The rule review is the real work.

What didn't move over

Three of Excalidraw's own rules have no built-in Oxlint version:

  1. no-restricted-syntax: Excalidraw uses it to stop plain text in JSX ("use t(...) instead"), which keeps the app translatable. That's a real guard you'd lose.
  2. import/order: Oxfmt can sort imports instead, but that's a formatting change, not a lint error.
  3. dot-notation: minor.

Oxlint's answer is JS plugins: you load the original ESLint plugin through Oxlint. That feature is still marked alpha. The other option is the official "run both" setup: oxlint && eslint, with eslint-plugin-oxlint turning off the rules Oxlint already covers.

One more trap: the automatic migration tool (@oxlint/migrate) only reads ESLint v9/v10 "flat" configs. Excalidraw still uses the old .eslintrc.json, so we ported its config by hand. If your project is on ESLint 8 or older, budget time for that too.

The formatter is the easy win

Oxfmt has its own migration command, and it worked on the first try:

npx oxfmt --migrate=prettier

It even caught a trap for us. Oxfmt's default line width is 100, while Prettier's is 80, and the tool kept Excalidraw at 80.

Oxfmt wanted to reformat 102 files (+1,163 / −1,092 lines). That sounds scary until you compare it with Prettier 3, which wants to change 126 files in the same repo. Every one of Oxfmt's 102 files was also on Prettier 3's list. So the churn comes from leaving Prettier 2's old style, not from Oxfmt being strange. You'd pay it either way.

Bonus: Prettier 2.6 can't even parse one of Excalidraw's TypeScript files (newer generic syntax). The team had added a "skip Prettier here" comment above it. Oxfmt read it fine.

What to do on Monday

  1. Got Prettier inside ESLint? Take it out (eslint-config-prettier stays, eslint-plugin-prettier goes). That's ~10 seconds saved per run, with no new tools.
  2. Try Oxfmt in a branch: npx oxfmt --migrate=prettier, then npx oxfmt. Commit the reformat as one separate commit and add its hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs, so git blame stays useful.
  3. Run Oxlint next to ESLint, not instead of it: npx oxlint first, read the warnings, and decide rule by rule. Replace ESLint only when nothing you rely on is left behind.

You'll be in good company. Bluesky's app already runs Oxlint as its lint script, and the Oxc docs list Sentry, Kibana, Electron and PostHog as users.

Desk verdict: Switch the formatter now; it's a near drop-in. Bring in the linter next to ESLint, and only remove ESLint after you've reviewed the rules, because the time goes into that review, not into waiting.

articles.title: I Built a Life Simulator That Deals You a Random Country at Birth — With Real UN Data
articles.description: Every life simulator starts the same way: you design your character. Pick a country, pick a family,...
articles.body_html:
Every life simulator starts the same way: you design your character. Pick a country, pick a family, optimize the stats. I wanted the opposite. Real life doesn't let you pick — you are dealt a country, a family, a body, at random, weighted by how many babies are actually born in each place. So I built a game around the deal itself: 1in8b.dev — "1 in 8 billion". You press one button, and you are born somewhere on Earth, with probabilities proportional to real birth counts. Then you live that life, year by year, until the local statistics say you don't.

The data layer

The whole game runs on public statistics for 172 countries and territories:

  • UN World Population Prospects for life tables and birth counts
  • WHO / World Bank indicators for life expectancy, under-5 mortality, income (GDP per capita, PPP), urbanization, fertility
  • Cause-of-death distributions per country — what people actually die of in Lagos is not what they die of in Osaka

That last one matters more than I expected. In the dataset, life expectancy runs from 54.5 years (Nigeria) to 85.5 (Hong Kong) — a 31-year gap determined almost entirely by the flag next to your birthplace. A simulation that ignores that is just a dice game. A simulation that uses it becomes something else: every run is a small lesson in how much of a "life outcome" is dealt before any choice is made. Mechanically, each in-game year rolls against the country's survival curve, its cause-of-death profile, and milestone events (schooling, work, migration, family) whose probabilities shift with the country's stats. Rich-country lives and poor-country lives don't just end at different ages — they have different shapes.

The build

It's a static site — vanilla JS, no framework, no backend, no accounts. All data ships as JSON and the simulation runs entirely in the browser. Two details from the build that might be useful to others:

1. Nine languages as static routes, not runtime switching. Each language is its own pre-built page (/ja/, /ko/, /fr/ …) with its own title, description, and canonical URL. The app detects the language from the path. This cost some duplication and bought a lot: every language version is independently indexable, and the first paint is already in the right language.

2. Country names are a real i18n problem. A UI string table is the easy part. But the game also needs the names of all 172 countries in every language — plus region names. We had Chinese, English, and Korean in the data; the other six languages were showing Chinese country names to French and Thai players. The fix was CLDR data (via Intl.DisplayNames) for the missing names, wired through one countryName() helper — and auditing ~250 hardcoded bilingual strings that had quietly bypassed the string table entirely. If your app "supports 9 languages," the long tail of strings outside the table is where it actually doesn't.

Try it

It's free, no sign-up, runs in the browser: 1in8b.dev

Play one life as yourself-by-birthplace, then re-roll and see who else you could have been. The second run is usually the one that sticks with you.

articles.title: How I Convert PDF to Markdown in the Browser
articles.description: I built a browser-based PDF to Markdown converter. I expected parsing the PDF to be the hard part. It...
articles.body_html:
I built a browser-based PDF to Markdown converter. I expected parsing the PDF to be the hard part. It wasn't: PDF.js handles that.

The hard part is that a PDF has no paragraphs, headings or lists. Word stores "this is Heading 2". HTML stores <h2>. A PDF stores "draw these glyphs at 16pt at (89.8, 751.4)". It's a list of drawing instructions for a printer.

So PDF to Markdown is reverse engineering: look at where text is drawn and how big it is, and guess the structure the author had in mind. This post walks through the rules I ended up with, with the real code, and the bugs that forced each one.

What PDF.js gives you

page.getTextContent() returns text items. Here's a simplified excerpt from page 1 of a real 4-page PDF:

{ "str": "Academic & Creative", "transform": [14, 0, 0, 14, 89.8, 188.6] }
{ "str": "", "transform": [16, 0, 0, 16, 89.8, 751.4], "hasEOL": true }
{ "str": "MD-to.com PDF Converter — Feature Guide", "transform": [16, 0, 0, 16, 89.8, 751.4] }
{ "str": "Download PDF", "transform": [11, 0, 0, 11, 376.7, 689.2] }
{ "str": "Try it now: paste any Markdown on the left and click", "transform": [11, 0, 0, 11, 89.8, 689.2] }

transform is a 2D matrix: the last two values are x and y, and the font size is in the first four. Things to notice:

  1. Item order isn't reading order. The first item is near the bottom of the page. "Download PDF" comes before "Try it now", but it's to its right on the same line.
  2. y points up. The origin is the bottom-left corner.
  3. Empty items carry nothing but a hasEOL flag.
  4. Font names are useless. fontName is an internal ID like g_d0_f1, so at this level you can't tell whether text is bold.

The pipeline 

PDF.js (parsing)
  └─ pdfjs-adapter: normalize coordinates → { str, x, y, width, height }
      └─ pdf-reader: per page, progress, cancel, isolate failed pages
          └─ pdf-extraction (pure functions):
               items → lines → drop headers/footers → body font size
               → headings / paragraphs / lists → escape → Markdown

The key design decision: the structure inference doesn't know about PDF.js. It takes plain { str, x, y, width, height } objects and returns a string. That made it testable with hand-written coordinates, which turned out to be the most valuable thing in the whole project.

The adapter flips the y axis to screen space (y grows downward) and takes the font size from the matrix, so scaled text gets its real size:

const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1 });
const transform = pdfjs.Util.transform(viewport.transform, item.transform);
return {
  str: item.str,
  x: transform[4],
  y: transform[5],
  width: item.width,
  height: Math.hypot(transform[2], transform[3]) || item.height,
};

Step 1: Items → lines

Drop empty items, sort by y then x, and put items on the same line when their y values are close:

Math.abs(last.y - item.y) <= Math.max(2, Math.min(last.height, item.height) * 0.3)

30% of the font size absorbs superscripts, baseline differences between fonts and floating-point noise, without merging two real lines.

When do you insert a space?

Generators split text however they like: per word, per glyph, or mid-word because of kerning or a font change. Joining with '' glues English words together. Joining with ' ' breaks words in half. So the joiner looks at the actual gap:

// Scripts written without spaces between words. Korean (Hangul) separates
// words with spaces, so it follows the same gap rules as Latin text.
const cjk = /[\p{Script=Han}\p{Script=Hiragana}\p{Script=Katakana}]/u;

function separator(left: string, right: string, gap?: number, height = 12) {
  if (!left || !right || /\s$/.test(left) || /^\s/.test(right)) return '';
  // Gap under 12% of the font size: one word split into two runs
  if (gap !== undefined && gap <= Math.max(0.5, height * 0.12)) return '';
  // No space before punctuation or after an opening bracket
  if (/^[，。！？、；：）》」』】〕,.!?;:)]/u.test(right) || /[（《「『【〔(]$/u.test(left))
    return '';
  if (cjk.test(left.at(-1)!) && cjk.test(right[0])) return '';
  return ' ';
}

Hel + lo with gap 0 → Hello. Hello + world with gap 6 → Hello world. Two Chinese runs → no space.

That comment about Korean is there because of a bug. The first version used "CJK" to mean Chinese, Japanese and Korean. But Korean separates words with spaces. I only caught it while testing a Korean PDF: 보고서를 + 작성합니다. came out as 보고서를작성합니다.

Even after the fix, one case can't be solved. Korean text can wrap between words or between syllables, and I generated both kinds of PDF in Chrome to compare. In both, the line ends with no trailing space and nothing in the data says "this break was mid-word". I chose to add a space across line breaks, because wrapping between words is more common. PDFs that wrap mid-word get an extra space at the break.

Step 2: Headers and footers

My first version deleted any line that was 1–4 digits or looked like Page 3 of 10. It deleted the year 2026 from body text and numbers from tables, and missed the actual running header, which wasn't a number.

Now each line gets a "margin key", and a key is only removed if it repeats across pages:

function marginKey(line: Line, page: PdfPageText): string | undefined {
  const relative = line.y / page.height;
  // Only the top or bottom 5% of the page, and only short lines
  if (!(relative < 0.05 || relative > 0.95) || line.text.length > 80) return;
  const edge = relative < 0.05 ? 'top' : 'bottom';
  const number =
    line.text.match(/^(?:page\s+)?(\d+)(?:\s+of\s+\d+)?$/i) ||
    line.text.match(/^-\s*(\d+)\s*-$/);
  if (number) {
    // Ambiguous numbers, years and amounts survive, even near a page edge.
    return Number(number[1]) === page.number ? `${edge}:page-number` : undefined;
  }
  return `${edge}:${Math.round(relative * 100)}:${line.text}`;
}

A key is removed only if it appears on at least max(2, ceil(pages × 0.6)) pages. Page numbers 3 on page 3 and 4 on page 4 share the key bottom:page-number, so they're removed together. A 2026 near the edge doesn't match the page number, so it stays.

This is deliberately conservative. Roman numerals and numbering that starts after the cover aren't removed. A leftover page number is obvious. A deleted sentence may never be noticed. The UI also tells the user how many header and footer lines were removed.

Step 3: Headings from font size

First, find the body font size, weighting each size by character count rather than line count, across the whole document:

function bodyFontSize(lines: Line[]) {
  const weights = new Map<number, number>();
  for (const line of lines) {
    const size = Math.round(line.height);
    weights.set(size, (weights.get(size) || 0) + line.text.length);
  }
  return [...weights].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0]?.[0] || 12;
}

Counting lines would let short headings and page numbers outvote long paragraphs. In the 4-page sample, 11pt had 2,146 characters, 10pt (code) 350, 16pt 184 and 14pt 119, so body text is 11pt.

Each line's size divided by the body size gives the heading level:

Ratio to body size Output
≥ 2 #
≥ 1.6 ##
> 1.3 ###
≤ 1.3 paragraph

In the sample, 16pt headings (ratio 1.45) became ###. The 14pt sub-headings (1.27) stayed as paragraphs. A lower threshold would catch them, but in another document with 10pt body and 12pt quotes, every quote would become a heading. No threshold fits every PDF, so this one leans careful, and the UI has a switch to turn heading detection off.

The feature that never worked

The first version also had bold detection: same size as body, short, bold → **sub-heading**. It checked whether the font name contained bold, heavy or black.

During the rewrite I realized this had never fired. Font names are g_d0_f1. I deleted it. A feature that looks like it works but doesn't is worse than no feature. Reading real font names from PDF.js font objects is on the list for later.

Step 4: Paragraphs and lists

Two signals start a new paragraph:

const verticalBreak = gap > Math.max(line.height, previous?.height || 0) * 1.8;
// Only a rightward shift is a first-line indent; returning to the left
// margin is the rest of that paragraph.
const paragraph = verticalBreak || (previous && line.x - previous.x > line.height);

Line spacing in body text is usually 1.2–1.5× the line height, and there's extra space between paragraphs, so 1.8× sits in between. Many documents, especially Chinese ones, use first-line indentation and no spacing at all. Only a shift to the right counts. The line after an indented first line moves left again, and that's the same paragraph. One version split every indented paragraph in two before I added that comment.

Lists start with •, ◦, -, *, 1., 1) and so on. The hard part is wrapped items:

• First item that wraps
  onto a second line        ← hanging indent: same item
• Second item
Independent text            ← back at the margin: not a list item

I got this wrong in both directions. Version one appended any line without a paragraph gap to the previous block, so Independent text was swallowed into the last list item. A later version split onto a second line into its own paragraph and broke the list in two.

The rule now: a line continues a list item if there's no vertical break and it starts to the right of the bullet:

} else if (
  last?.kind === 'list' &&
  !verticalBreak &&
  line.x - last.x! > Math.max(1, line.height * 0.2)
) {
  // Hanging-indent line continues the current list item.

Output:

- First item that wraps onto a second line
- Second item

Independent text

Step 5: Escaping, but not too much

Text in a PDF is literal. # tag at the start of a line is a hashtag, not a heading. The first version escaped nothing, so lines starting with # became headings, <b>literal</b> rendered as bold, and a line like --- | --- turned the line above it into a table header.

Escaping every Markdown character caused a different bug: citations like [1] rendered as math. My renderer supports KaTeX, and \[ ... \] is the display math delimiter. A standard escaper turns [1] into \[1\], which most renderers show as [1]. Mine showed an equation.

So the escaper only touches characters in positions where they would trigger syntax:

export function escapePdfText(text: string) {
  const escaped = text
    .replace(/[\\`*$]/g, '\\$&')
    // Only underscores that could start emphasis; snake_case stays as is
    .replace(/(?<![\p{L}\p{N}])_|_(?![\p{L}\p{N}])/gu, '\\_')
    .replace(/~(?=~)|(?<=~)~/g, '\\~')
    // `]` only before ( [ : — links, images, references. `[` is never escaped.
    .replace(/\](?=[([:])/g, '\\]')
    .replace(/\^(?=\[)/g, '\\^')
    .replace(/<(?=[\p{L}/!?])/gu, '\\<')
    .replace(/&(?=#\d+;|#x[\da-f]+;|[a-z][\da-z]*;)/gi, '\\&')
    // Line-start blocks: headings, quotes, lists, setext underlines and rules
    .replace(/^(?:#|>|[-+](?=\s|$)|[-=](?=[-=\s]*$))/, '\\$&')
    .replace(/^(\d+)([.)])(?=\s|$)/, '$1\\$2');
  // A delimiter row such as `--- | ---` would turn the previous line into a table
  return /^[\s|:\\-]*\|[\s|:\\-]*$/.test(escaped) && escaped.includes('-')
    ? escaped.replace(/\|/g, '\\|')
    : escaped;
}

snake_case, C#, AT&T, 5 > 3 and [1] pass through unchanged. A line starting with 1. becomes 1\. so it doesn't turn into a list.

The test for this renders escaped strings with the site's own Markdown renderer and checks that the output text matches the input. Testing against a generic renderer wouldn't have caught [1], because that bug only exists with KaTeX enabled.

Step 6: Never compare coordinates across pages

The first version concatenated lines from all pages and then grouped paragraphs. But every page's coordinates start from zero. If the last line of page 1 was at y = 680 and the first line of page 2 was also at 680, the gap was 0, and the two pages became one paragraph.

Now every page is rendered on its own and joined with a blank line:

// Never compare Y coordinates or merge paragraphs across page boundaries.
markdown: filtered
  .map((page) => renderPage(page, bodySize, options))
  .filter(Boolean)
  .join('\n\n'),

The trade-off: a paragraph that continues on the next page gets split. Deleting one blank line fixes that. Two unrelated pages merged into one paragraph is much harder to spot.

Testing a guessing algorithm

Heuristics have one big risk: fixing one case breaks another. Since the inference is pure, every bug above became a test with hand-written coordinates, run with Node's built-in node:test:

const item = (str, y = 100, x = 30, width = str.length * 6) =>
  ({ str, y, x, width, height: 12 });

test('glyph runs infer word gaps without splitting adjacent characters', () => {
  assert.equal(
    extractPdfLines([item('Hello', 100, 30, 30), item('world', 100, 66)])[0].text,
    'Hello world',
  );
  assert.equal(
    extractPdfLines([item('Hel', 100, 30, 18), item('lo', 100, 48)])[0].text,
    'Hello',
  );
});

There are tests for each bug in this post: years surviving the margin filter, Korean spacing, first-line indents, list items swallowing paragraphs, [1] turning into math, --- | --- creating a table, and equal coordinates on different pages.

A second layer builds tiny but valid PDF files in code (a few objects plus an xref table) and runs them through the real PDF.js. That catches the other class of bug, where the pure function is right but PDF.js returns data different from what I assumed.

A few engineering details

  • One bad page doesn't fail the document. A page that throws is marked failed, the rest still convert, and the status bar lists failed pages and pages with no text (scans or blank pages) instead of a generic error.
  • Cancellation. Every async step races against a cancel promise, the PDF.js loading task is destroyed exactly once, and the loop yields with setTimeout(0) after each page so large files don't freeze the tab.
  • The worker is bundled, not loaded from a CDN, so its version always matches the installed PDF.js.

What coordinates can't tell you

  • Tables come out as rows of text. There's no border or column-alignment analysis.
  • Multi-column layouts get interleaved, because items at the same y become one line.
  • Hyphenated line breaks like inter- / national come out as inter- national. There's no reliable way to tell layout hyphens from real ones, so I don't guess.
  • Code indentation, formula structure and images aren't in the text layer in a recoverable form.
  • Scanned PDFs have no text layer and need OCR.

Marker, MinerU and Docling solve these with layout and OCR models, and they do it better. They also need a Python environment or a server upload. This converter goes the other way: rules only, in the browser, no upload, results in seconds for ordinary text PDFs. They're tools for different jobs.

Next on the list, each only once there are enough counter-examples in the tests: real font weights for bold, merging paragraphs across pages when the first page's line has no closing punctuation and the next starts lowercase, column detection from vertical whitespace bands, and simple table recovery from stable x alignment.

The question behind every rule

Almost every bug came from one wrong assumption: reading a PDF as a structured document. It's drawing instructions. So every rule answers one question: if this guess is wrong, what does it cost the user?

  • Headers and footers: keep a page number rather than delete a sentence
  • Headings: miss a heading rather than promote every quote
  • Pages: split a paragraph rather than merge two pages
  • Escaping: escape only what triggers syntax, so [1] stays [1]
  • Bold detection: a broken feature is worse than none

The converter is free at https://md-to.com/pdf-to-markdown and runs entirely in your browser. If you have a text PDF it gets wrong, tell me about it in the comments. Every counter-example becomes a test case.

articles.title: The halo around a blurred video background is the dark-fringe bug from texture filtering
articles.description: I zoomed into a blurred-background export from a browser video matting tool and found a dark ring...
articles.body_html:
I zoomed into a blurred-background export from a browser video matting tool and found a dark ring around the speaker's head. My first suspect was the matte, and it turned out not to be the cause. At the graphics-tool company I worked at before, dark fringes around resized transparent PNG icons came in as bug reports every few months. This ring is the same bug in a different place: a blur filter is averaging pixels that belong to another layer. Both standard fixes from texture work carry over, and on one clip I measured how far each gets.

The ring is the person blurred into the background

I used ImgIng's video matting (https://imging.ai/) for the export, a Beta that runs in desktop Chrome or Edge and not on phones. I only saw its output, not its code. The clip is an 8-second, 478×850 sign language video from Wikimedia Commons (Sayvhior, CC BY-SA 4.0, signing by JudithNG12), one woman in a headscarf before a light curtain. I exported it with blur strength 18 (the default) and 40 in Chromium 149 on a desktop machine that had no GPU acceleration. In its blur-original-background mode the ring appears because what gets blurred is the original frame with the person still in it, so the dark of her clothes and skin spreads past her outline. To put numbers on it I compared brightness in rings outside her edge, on four frames, against an empty-curtain reference rebuilt from the clip itself; it covers 62.5% of the frame. Right at her edge, in the first 4 px, the background read 67.8 grey levels (0 to 255) darker than it should at strength 18, and 63.1 darker at 40. The visible part stretched about 16 to 32 px out at 18 and beyond 32 px at 40.

Filtered transparent textures get the same dark fringe

Take a sprite stored with straight alpha, where the fully transparent pixels still hold some colour, usually black. Scale it and the filter averages those invisible black pixels into the edge, leaving a dark outline that was never in the artwork. Background blur does the same thing with the layers swapped. The kernel should only see background, but it reaches across her edge and pulls her colour in. Real-time depth of field hits it too, where a sharp foreground leaks into the blurred background unless samples are weighted by depth. Texture pipelines settled on two fixes: premultiply, so excluded pixels carry zero weight, or bleed the edge colours outward into the empty area before filtering.

Both texture fixes work on video frames

I reproduced both with OpenCV on the same frames, taking the matte from a transparent export of the clip (WebM only in that tool). Here is the core, trimmed. It's a generic compositing order, not a feature of the tool.

# r is the blur strength, 18 or 40
keep = 1.0 - matte                                  # how much of each pixel is background
smear = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0, 0), r)            # blur everything, person included
num = cv2.GaussianBlur(img * keep[..., None], (0, 0), r)
den = cv2.GaussianBlur(keep, (0, 0), r)[..., None]
weighted = num / np.maximum(den, 1e-3)              # premultiplied-style blur
grow4 = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (9, 9))
fill_zone = cv2.dilate((matte > 0.02).astype(np.uint8), grow4)   # fill area grown 4 px
plate = cv2.GaussianBlur(cv2.inpaint(img_u8, fill_zone * 255, 9, cv2.INPAINT_TELEA), (0, 0), r)
out = img * matte[..., None] + plate * keep[..., None]     # sharp person on top

The weighted version is premultiplication written out: blur colour times weight, blur the weight, divide. Averaged over the four frames on the original matte, it left −0.1 to −1.6 grey levels across the rings at strength 18, and −1.3 to −3.3 at 40. Filling first, which is edge bleeding by inpainting, landed within ±1 at both strengths. I haven't pinned down where the weighted version's leftover comes from; at 40 it is still a few levels, which I would not ship as a regression baseline without knowing why.

Filling has to reach past the matte

Texture bleeding runs a few pixels past the visible edge, and the fill here needs that margin too. With a matte shrunk 2 px to a hard edge and the fill area taken straight from it, her outer 2 px stayed in the background, got blurred, and at strength 18 the 4 to 16 px rings came back at −14.1. Growing the fill 4 px past the matte brought them to +0.3. The plain blur-everything version sat at −15.4 on the original matte. Filling does cost an inpainting pass on every frame, which the weighted blur avoids.

Read the last group first: with the hard edge, the fill taken straight from the matte sinks almost as low as blurring everything, while the grown fill sits back at zero. Data: my own measurements on this clip, four frames.

A thin dark line is a different member of the family

My filled frames still show a very thin dark outline right on her edge. I read it as the other straight-alpha problem: edge pixels already contain the old background mixed into their colour, so the curtain or the dark wall rides along when she is pasted onto anything new. Removing it is colour decontamination, a separate step I didn't measure. So in a compositing pipeline I'd place it this way: the blur stage only ever receives background pixels, through weights or a fill, and decontaminating the edge is its own stage between matting and the final paste.

articles.title: I built 190+ free online tools that don't upload your files
articles.description: Hi, I'm Fayaz, a web developer from Karachi, Pakistan.  Like most people, I keep needing small file...
articles.body_html:
Hi, I'm Fayaz, a web developer from Karachi, Pakistan.

Like most people, I keep needing small file jobs done: shrink a photo, merge a few PDFs, convert a Word file, format some JSON. And every time, the free tools I found came with a catch:

  • a watermark on the result,
  • a sign-up wall before the download,
  • a limit of two files a day unless I paid,
  • or they wanted me to upload private documents to a server I knew nothing about.

So a month ago I started building ToolsBench: one place where these everyday jobs are free, simple, and done properly. It now has more than 190 tools across images, PDFs, documents, video, audio, text, code and more.

The main idea: do the work in the browser

Modern browsers are powerful enough to do most file processing locally. If the work happens on your device, there's nothing to upload, nothing to store, and nothing to leak. It's also faster, because you skip the upload and download round trip.

Here's what does the heavy lifting:

Job Library
Merge, split, rotate PDFs pdf-lib
Render PDF pages (PDF to image) PDF.js
Video and audio conversion ffmpeg.wasm
Text from images (OCR) Tesseract.js
HEIC (iPhone photos) to JPG heic2any
Word documents mammoth, docx
Excel and CSV SheetJS
Compress and resize images the Canvas API
QR codes and barcodes qrcode, JsBarcode, ZXing

A few tools genuinely need a server, such as an IP address lookup. Those say so clearly at the top of the page, so you always know where your data goes.

The stack

  • Next.js (App Router) with React and Tailwind CSS
  • Prisma with Turso (SQLite at the edge) for tool pages, blog posts and FAQs, edited from a small admin panel
  • Hosted on Netlify, DNS on Cloudflare

Things I learned along the way

1. ffmpeg.wasm is amazing, but heavy. The core is tens of megabytes, so it only loads when you open a video or audio tool, and it's cached long-term after the first visit. Nobody should download a video encoder just to format some JSON.

2. Lazy-load everything. With 190+ tools, each tool's code (and its libraries) only loads on its own page. The home page stays fast even though the whole site uses a lot of libraries.

3. Big files need care. Browsers have memory limits, especially on phones. Loading libraries only when a file is actually processed, and releasing object URLs once a download is done, keeps things from slowing down.

4. Hosting adds surprises. My host injected a small HTML comment into the page <head>, which broke React hydration in production only. It took some bisecting to find. If you see a hydration error that you can't reproduce locally, check what your host adds to the HTML.

What's next

I'm adding tools step by step, and I write short guides that explain what each tool can and can't do.

If you try it, I'd love to hear what's missing or broken. Feedback from developers is the most useful kind I can get.

👉 toolsbench.net

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: DORA for Financial-Sector Suppliers: Essential Preparations for ICT Providers
articles.description: Understand the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and prep your ICT services for compliance in the financial sector.
articles.body_html:
Introduction

The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is a significant legislative measure aimed at ensuring that the financial sector is resilient against IT disruptions. As a financial-sector supplier, particularly those providing Information and Communication Technology (ICT) services, understanding DORA's implications and preparing accordingly is crucial. This article outlines necessary actions for ICT providers under DORA to ensure compliance and foster resilience in their services.

What is DORA?

DORA aims to strengthen the IT resilience of the European financial space. It is designed to address challenges posed by increasing digitalization in the sector, ensuring a comprehensive approach to operational resilience. Its requirements cover various aspects, including risk management, testing, and reporting, effectively shaping the regulatory landscape in which ICT suppliers operate.

Understanding DORA’s Core Requirements

DORA introduces several key regulations that ICT providers must adhere to:

1. Risk Management Frameworks

Providers need to develop comprehensive risk management frameworks that identify, assess, and manage ICT risks effectively. This involves:

  • Conducting regular risk assessments.
  • Establishing governance structures that include accountability for digital resilience.
  • Defining risk appetite and tolerance levels.

2. Incident Reporting

ICT providers must implement effective incident detection and reporting mechanisms. The requirements include:

  • The establishment of protocols for detection, management, and reporting of ICT-related incidents.
  • Timely notification of incidents to relevant authorities and stakeholders, ideally within 24 hours.

3. Testing and Validation of Resilience

DORA mandates that ICT suppliers perform regular testing of their operational resilience. Recommended practices include:

  • Conducting stress tests and scenario analyses to assess the robustness of systems.
  • Implementing a framework for coordination with financial institutions during testing phases to ensure alignment and understanding.

4. Third-party Risk Management

ICT suppliers must also have strategies in place to manage third-party risks. This involves:

  • Due diligence assessments of vendors to evaluate their operational resilience.
  • Continuous monitoring of third-party risks throughout the relationship.

Steps to Prepare for DORA Compliance

Preparing for DORA compliance entails several action steps that ICT providers must undertake:

1. Conduct a Gap Assessment

Start with a comprehensive gap assessment to understand your current standing in relation to DORA requirements. Identify areas where your processes and controls may fall short. This assessment should ideally include:

  • A review of existing policies and procedures.
  • Identification of compliance gaps, including both technical and procedural weaknesses.

2. Enhance Your Risk Management Framework

Based on findings from the gap assessment, enhance your risk management framework to meet DORA’s expectations. Focus on:

  • Integrating IT risk management with overall business risk management.
  • Documenting processes clearly and establishing accountability for risk management tasks.

3. Develop Incident Management Protocols

Establish incident management protocols that align with DORA’s requirements. Ensure that your protocols include:

  • Clear definitions of what constitutes an incident.
  • Procedures for timely communication and escalation within the organization.

4. Implement Continuous Monitoring Practices

DORA requires that ICT providers have mechanisms in place for continuous monitoring of their ICT systems. This may include:

  • Deployment of automated monitoring tools to detect anomalies.
  • Regular audits and reviews to assess the effectiveness of existing controls and processes.

Cross-Framework Mapping

Understanding how DORA aligns with other regulatory frameworks is essential for ICT suppliers working in multiple jurisdictions. Cross-framework mapping can help:

  • Identify overlapping requirements between DORA, ISO 27001, SOC 2, and other standards, enabling organizations to streamline their compliance efforts.
  • Reduce redundancy and overlap in efforts to establish a cohesive compliance strategy.

Security Testing for Compliance

Regular security testing is vital for demonstrating compliance with DORA. Consider the following:

  • Engage in penetration testing programs to simulate real-world attacks and evaluate system vulnerabilities.
  • Regularly conduct vulnerability assessments to identify and remediate security weaknesses in a timely manner.

Evidence and Audit Preparation

Preparing for potential audits requires documenting compliance efforts thoroughly. Key activities include:

  • Collecting evidence that demonstrates adherence to DORA requirements.
  • Maintaining an organized record of policies, risk assessments, incident reports, and security testing outcomes.

The Role of Bitkosh Technologies

While this article has focused on the necessary preparations for ICT providers under DORA, organizations may benefit from professional guidance. Bitkosh Technologies specializes in compliance readiness and can assist in gap assessments, cross-framework mappings, and evidence preparation. Such support can enhance your operational processes and increase the likelihood of a successful audit.

Conclusion

As the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) comes into effect, ICT providers serving the financial sector must take proactive steps to prepare. Understanding its core requirements and implementing the necessary framework adjustments are crucial for compliance and operational resilience. By engaging in proactive risk management, effective incident response planning, and targeted security testing, ICT providers can not only comply with DORA but also contribute to a more resilient financial ecosystem.
